# How to use this guide

Regulatory Affairs (MPH104T) is a descriptive, fact-heavy subject. Marks come from knowing **which law, which form, which authority and which timeline** applies, and from presenting procedures as clean flow charts and comparison tables. There is little calculation; the only formula you may be asked is the dissolution similarity factor f2. Study one unit a day: read the notes, close them, redraw every flow chart (ANDA review, NDA steps, foreign registration, global submission, protocol development, ethics committee working, informed consent, safety reporting) from memory, then do the question bank and MCQs for that unit.

**How the notes follow the syllabus.** The PCI syllabus has four units. Unit 1 is very large (part a: documentation and generic development; part b: product approval requirements), so it is split here into two units. The mapping is:

| These notes | PCI syllabus |
| --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Documentation and generic drug product development | Unit 1(a) |
| Unit 2 Regulatory requirements for product approval | Unit 1(b) |
| Unit 3 CMC, post-approval changes, combination products and devices, CTD/eCTD, FDA liaison, ICH, EU/MHRA/TGA/ROW | Unit 2 |
| Unit 4 Non-clinical development, global IND/NDA/ANDA, IMPD, IB | Unit 3 |
| Unit 5 Clinical trials, IRB/IEC, informed consent, HIPAA, pharmacovigilance | Unit 4 |

Nothing has been left out or moved between syllabus units. Indian requirements (CDSCO, NDCT Rules 2019, Medical Devices Rules 2017) are added where they help comparison, because Indian universities often ask "compare with India". Several topics overlap with the B.Pharm courses BP702T (Industrial Pharmacy II) and BP804ET (Pharmaceutical Regulatory Science); the facts match those notes.

**Exam pattern (end-semester theory, 75 marks, 3 hours).** The PCI M.Pharm scheme gives MPH104T 100 marks: 25 internal assessment + 75 end-semester, 3 hours. PCI does not prescribe sections for M.Pharm papers, so this pack uses the common PCI 75-mark split (used for M.Pharm by, for example, Bahra University, Shimla). Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long answers — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. Very short ones are quick definitions that also help with MCQs and with internal tests.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a standard question in most papers on this syllabus; prepare the full answer with a chart or table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years, or as part of a larger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Documentation and generics | MFR contents, DMF types and LoA, Hatch-Waxman Act (Paragraph IV, 30-month stay, 180-day exclusivity), CFR Title 21 parts, f2 and BCS biowaiver, BE study design and 80–125%, ANDA process, SUPAC levels, PMS reporting, outsourcing BE to CROs |
| 2 Product approval requirements | API requirements (ICH Q7, DMF), BLA and biosimilars (351(a), 351(k), Purple Book), expedited programmes, NDA steps and meetings, US registration of foreign drugs, NDA vs ANDA vs BLA |
| 3 CMC to ROW | CMC (Module 3), PAS/CBE-30/CBE-0/annual report, EU variations, combination products and PMOA, device classes and 510(k)/PMA, CTD modules, eCTD features, FDA liaison, ICH Q/S/E/M, EMA procedures, MHRA, TGA, ROW requirements |
| 4 Non-clinical and global submissions | Non-clinical study package (S7A core battery, S2 battery, two species), GLP, ICH M3(R2), first human dose, IND contents and 30-day rule, EU CTR/CTIS, IMPD, Investigator's Brochure |
| 5 Clinical trials | Protocol contents, EC formation (India vs USA) and working, informed consent elements and special cases, HIPAA authorization and de-identification, SAE reporting (24 h/14 days; 7/15 days), DSMB, causality |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Open every answer with a one-line definition and the legal basis ("An ANDA is filed under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act; rules in 21 CFR 314.94").
2. Expand every abbreviation the first time (CMC, PMOA, IMPD, IB, SUSAR, PHI, CTIS, RLD, SUPAC, GDUFA).
3. Use flow charts for processes and tables for comparisons (NDA vs ANDA vs BLA; IND vs CTA; IB vs IMPD; IRB vs Indian EC; US device classes vs Indian classes; EU procedures).
4. Learn the fixed numbers exactly: NCE 5 years, new clinical investigation 3 years, orphan 7 years, paediatric 6 months, 180-day exclusivity, 30-month stay, biologic reference exclusivity 12 years; IND 30 days; NDA filing 60 days, review 10/6 months; EU 210 active days + 67 days; 15-day alert reports, quarterly for 3 years then annual, records 10 years; ICH 7/15 days; India SAE 24 hours/14 days, 90/30 working days, EC ≥ 7 members, PSURs 6-monthly × 2 years then yearly × 2 years; HIPAA 18 identifiers; f2 50–100; BE 90% CI 80.00–125.00%.
5. Postgraduate examiners reward depth: after the basic list, add one line on "current trend" (ICH E6(R3), eCTD v4.0, ICH Q12, EU CTR 536/2014) or on the Indian position.
6. Rules change. In an answer it is fine to say "as per the NDCT Rules, 2019" or "as per 21 CFR 312"; in real work always read the current text on cdsco.gov.in, fda.gov, ema.europa.eu or ich.org.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, prepare these with a chart or table each: **Hatch-Waxman and ANDA process**, **DMF types**, **BE study design**, **NDA steps**, **BLA vs biosimilar**, **post-approval change categories**, **combination products (PMOA)**, **CTD/eCTD**, **ICH Q/S/E/M**, **IND contents**, **IMPD and IB**, **ethics committee and informed consent**, **SAE reporting**.

**Unit 1 — Documentation and generics**

| Topic | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| Documents | Quality manual/SMF → specs, MFR, SOPs → BMR/BPR → records; ALCOA+; Schedule M; 21 CFR 211 |
| MFR | Product identity, formula with overages, equipment, process steps, IPCs, yields, packaging, approvals |
| DMF | Confidential; LoA; not approved on its own; Types II API, III packaging, IV excipient, V reference (I discontinued); EU ASMF/CEP |
| Distribution records | Batch → consignee; recall Classes I–III |
| Hatch-Waxman 1984 | 505(j) ANDA; patent term restoration; safe harbour; Paragraph I–IV; suit in 45 days → 30-month stay; 180-day exclusivity |
| Exclusivity | NCE 5 y; new clinical investigation 3 y; orphan 7 y; paediatric +6 months; CGT 180 days |
| Amendments | MMA 2003, FDAAA 2007, FDASIA/GDUFA 2012, FDARA 2017; BPCI Act 2009 |
| CFR Title 21 | 11, 50, 54, 56, 58, 210/211, 312, 314, 320, 600s, 800s |

| SUPAC | Level 1 annual report; Level 2 CBE/PAS; Level 3 PAS (+BE) |
| PMS (314.80) | 15-day alert; quarterly × 3 y (30 days after quarter) then annual (60 days); records 10 y |
| CRO | Audit, contract, quality agreement; sponsor stays responsible |

**Unit 2 — Product approval requirements**

- API: ICH Q7; DMF; registration and listing (21 CFR 207); Q3A/Q3C/Q3D/M7.
- BLA 351(a): safe, pure, potent; 21 CFR 600–680. Biosimilar 351(k): no clinically meaningful difference; interchangeable; 12-year reference exclusivity; Purple Book.
- Expedited: fast track (rolling review), breakthrough, accelerated approval (surrogate + confirmatory), priority (6 months), RMAT; orphan < 200,000.
- NDA: 505(b)(1)/(b)(2); 356h; Type A/B/C meetings; 60-day filing; day-74 letter; 10/6 months; PLR label; REMS.
- Foreign registration: DUNS → establishment registration + listing (US agent) → eCTD + fees → PAI → import admissibility; 483, warning letter, import alert.
- India: CT-04 → CT-06; CT-18 import; CT-21 manufacture; 90/30 working days; SUGAM; SEC.

**Unit 3 — CMC to ROW**

| Topic | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| CMC | Module 3: 3.2.S, 3.2.P (P.2 development), 3.2.A, 3.2.R; QOS 2.3 |
| US changes | PAS / CBE-30 / CBE-0 / annual report (314.70, 314.97, 601.12); annual report within 60 days of anniversary; ICH Q12 |
| EU variations | IA (do and tell), IA-IN, IB (tell-wait-do), II (prior approval), extension |
| Combination products | 4 types (3.2(e)); PMOA (3.2(m)); OCP; RFD; Part 4 |
| Devices USA | I (general), II (special; 510(k)), III (PMA); De Novo; HDE; IDE |
| Devices EU / India | MDR 2017/745 I, IIa, IIb, III, CE mark; India MDR 2017 A–D (SLA A/B; CLA C/D + imports) |
| CTD / eCTD | M4; 5 modules, M1 regional; eCTD M8: m1–m5, XML backbone, sequences, new/replace/append/delete, checksums |
| ICH | Q1–Q14; S1–S12; E1–E19 (E6 GCP R3 2025); M1 MedDRA, M3, M4, M7, M8, M9, M10, M13; CDSCO is an observer |

| UK / Australia | MHRA: IRP, Yellow Card; TGA: ARTG, AUST R/L, CTN/CTA |
| ROW | ACTD 4 parts; GCC; WHO PQ; COPP; zone IV stability; local agent and labels |

**Unit 4 — Non-clinical and global submissions**

- Safety pharmacology core battery: CNS, CVS, respiratory (S7A); QT S7B/E14.
- Toxicology: single/repeat dose in rodent + non-rodent; S2 genotoxicity battery; S1, S5, S6 (relevant species), S9; timing M3(R2).
- GLP: 21 CFR 58; OECD; NGCMA India. First dose: NOAEL → HED → ÷ safety factor (default 10); MABEL.
- IND 312.23(a): 1571, contents, IB, protocols, CMC, pharm/tox, prior human experience; 1572; 30 days; clinical hold.
- EU CTR 536/2014: 31 Jan 2022; CTIS compulsory 31 Jan 2023; transition end 31 Jan 2025; Part I / Part II.
- IMPD: quality (S + P) + summaries; phase-appropriate; simplified IMPD.
- IB: summary, introduction, properties, non-clinical, effects in humans, guidance; RSI; reviewed at least yearly.

questions.answer:
1. Name and basis: Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act, 1984; amended the FD&C Act; a balance between generic access and innovator incentives.
2. For generics: created the ANDA route under section 505(j) — no repeat of safety/efficacy trials; sameness + bioequivalence to the reference listed drug (RLD).
3. Safe harbour: using a patented drug to generate data for FDA submission is not infringement, so development can start before patent expiry.
4. Patent certifications: Paragraph I (no patent), II (expired), III (will expire on date), IV (invalid/not infringed); section viii carve-out of method-of-use patents.
5. Paragraph IV: notice to patent owner; suit within 45 days triggers an automatic 30-month stay of approval; first successful filer earns 180-day generic exclusivity.
6. For innovators: patent term restoration for time lost in FDA review; Orange Book patent listing; data exclusivities — NCE 5 years (Paragraph IV ANDA allowed after 4 years), new clinical investigation 3 years.
7. Amendments: MMA 2003 (one 30-month stay per ANDA, forfeiture of 180-day exclusivity); FDAAA 2007 (citizen petition rules, REMS); FDASIA 2012 (GDUFA user fees and review goals); FDARA 2017 (competitive generic therapy, 180-day exclusivity); BPCI Act 2009 extended the idea to biosimilars (351(k)).
8. Impact: generics became the majority of US prescriptions; Indian firms became major ANDA and DMF filers; patent strategy is now part of product selection.
9. Conclusion: development decisions (timing, Paragraph IV, formulation design-around) depend on the Orange Book patents and exclusivities created by this Act.
questions.question: Discuss the Hatch-Waxman Act, 1984 and its later amendments. How did it shape generic drug product development in the USA?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: ANDA (section 505(j); 21 CFR 314.94) — application for a generic shown same as and bioequivalent to the RLD.
2. Requirements: RLD and reference standard identified; same active ingredient, dosage form, strength, route, conditions of use; labelling same as RLD; BE; full CMC with stability; patent certifications; GMP; GDUFA fees.
3. Flow: ANDA in eCTD → receipt/filing review (refuse-to-receive if incomplete; DMF completeness checked) → discipline reviews (BE, drug substance via DMF, drug product, microbiology, labelling) → pre-approval inspections of manufacturing and BE sites → information requests → action: approval, tentative approval (blocked only by patents/exclusivity) or complete response letter. Reviewed by the Office of Generic Drugs, CDER.
4. BE design: randomised two-period, two-sequence crossover, single dose, healthy volunteers (patients for toxic drugs), washout ≥5 half-lives, fasting and often fed studies as per product-specific guidance.
5. Sampling to define Cmax and cover AUC; validated bioanalytical method (ICH M10).
6. Parameters: Cmax (rate), AUC0–t, AUC0–∞ (extent), Tmax.
7. Statistics: log-transformed data, ANOVA; 90% confidence interval of test/reference geometric mean ratio within 80.00–125.00% for Cmax and AUC.
8. Special cases: highly variable drugs (reference-scaled BE), narrow therapeutic index drugs, steady-state, clinical endpoint studies; biowaivers (BCS, lower strengths).
9. Outcome: therapeutic equivalence rating (e.g., AB) in the Orange Book.
questions.question: Describe the ANDA regulatory approval process. Add a note on bioequivalence study design and acceptance criteria.

questions.answer:
1. Need: exhibit/bio batches are small; after approval firms scale up, change sites, equipment, suppliers or process.
2. SUPAC guidances: SUPAC-IR, SUPAC-MR, SUPAC-SS; classify changes in components and composition, site, batch size, equipment and process.
3. Level 1: unlikely to have detectable effect → annual report; compendial tests, stability of one batch.
4. Level 2: could have significant effect → CBE or prior approval supplement depending on change; multi-point dissolution comparison, stability.
5. Level 3: likely significant effect → prior approval supplement; dissolution, stability, often in vivo BE.
6. Example: SUPAC-IR batch size increase above 10 × pilot/bio-batch is Level 2.
7. Legal basis: 21 CFR 314.70 (NDA), 314.97 (ANDA): PAS, CBE-30, CBE-0, annual report.
8. PMS purpose: detect rare, delayed ADRs, interactions, effects in special populations.
9. US 21 CFR 314.80: 15-day alert report for serious unexpected experiences; periodic reports quarterly for 3 years (within 30 days of quarter end) then annually (within 60 days of anniversary); records 10 years; also MedWatch/FAERS, REMS, Phase IV commitments, Sentinel.
10. India: PSURs six-monthly for 2 years then yearly for 2 years (NDCT Rules 2019); PvPI coordinated by IPC Ghaziabad.
questions.question: Explain scale-up and post-approval changes (SUPAC). Add a note on post-marketing surveillance requirements for an approved drug.

questions.answer:
1. DMF: confidential document filed with FDA by a manufacturer giving details of facilities, processes or materials used for a drug component.
2. FDA does not approve or disapprove it; reviews it when an application cites it.
3. Types: II drug substance/intermediate/drug product; III packaging; IV excipients, colourants, flavours; V FDA-accepted reference information; Type I (site) no longer used.
4. Letter of Authorisation: holder authorises FDA to refer to the DMF for a named applicant; applicant cites DMF number + LoA in its ANDA/NDA; confidential data stay with FDA.
5. Holder keeps it current (amendments, annual updates); EU equivalents ASMF and CEP.
questions.question: What is a Drug Master File? Give its types and the role of the Letter of Authorisation.

questions.answer:
1. Product name, strength, dosage form, code, batch size, shelf life.
2. Prepared, checked, approved signatures with dates; version.
3. Formula: each ingredient, grade, quantity per unit and per batch, overages with reason.
4. Equipment list and line clearance.
5. Step-by-step manufacturing instructions with process parameters.
6. In-process controls with limits; theoretical yield and limits.
7. Packaging materials, instructions, specimen labels; storage and precautions; sampling for QC.
questions.question: List the contents of a Master Formula Record.

questions.answer:
1. CFR: codification of permanent rules of US federal agencies first published in the Federal Register; 50 titles.
2. Title 21 — Food and Drugs (FDA). Citation: 21 CFR 314.94 = Title 21, Part 314, Section 94.
3. Part 11 electronic records/signatures; Part 50 informed consent; 54 financial disclosure; 56 IRBs; 58 GLP.
4. 210/211 cGMP; 312 IND; 314 NDA/ANDA; 320 BA/BE; 600–680 biologics; 800 onwards devices.
5. eCFR updated continuously; guidance documents explain current thinking but are not binding.
questions.question: What is the Code of Federal Regulations? Name important parts of Title 21.

questions.answer:
1. Dissolution as the in vitro measure of drug release.
2. Discriminating method: apparatus, media (pH 1.2, 4.5, 6.8), volume, speed, time points.
3. Profile comparison with RLD by f2; f2 50–100 = similar (≤10% average difference).
4. BCS classes I–IV; BCS-based biowaiver for Class I (and Class III with conditions) IR products (ICH M9).
5. Lower-strength biowaivers with proportional composition; IVIVC Level A supports changes in MR products.
questions.question: Explain in vitro assessment of drug product performance for generic products.

questions.answer:
1. CROs provide clinical unit, bioanalysis, biostatistics, regulatory writing.
2. Steps: needs → shortlist → confidentiality agreement → proposal → qualification audit → contract + quality agreement → study → report → sponsor audit.
3. Selection points: regulator inspection history, registration with CDSCO and registered EC, validated ICH M10 methods, Part 11 systems, volunteer database, independent QA.
4. Sponsor oversight via monitoring and audits.
5. ICH E6: duties can be transferred, but sponsor remains ultimately responsible; data integrity failures can lead to rejection of studies.
questions.question: Discuss outsourcing of BA/BE studies to contract research organisations.

questions.answer: A batch-wise record of where each product lot was dispatched (consignee, quantity, date, invoice). It allows quick, complete recall and complaint tracing.
questions.question: What is a distribution record and why is it kept?

questions.answer: The 90% confidence interval of the test/reference geometric mean ratio, on log-transformed data, must lie within 80.00–125.00%.
questions.question: State the acceptance criterion for bioequivalence of Cmax and AUC.

questions.answer:
1. Biological product: vaccine, blood product, toxin, antitoxin, protein, etc.; made in living systems; process defines product.
2. BLA under section 351(a) of PHS Act; 21 CFR 600–680; standard: safe, pure and potent; facility must assure this; Form 356h.
3. Centres: CBER (vaccines, blood, cell/gene therapy), CDER (most monoclonal antibodies and therapeutic proteins).
4. Extra content: cell banks, viral safety, process validation, comparability, lot release, establishment description; licence number on label.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Documentation in industry and generic drug product development

This unit covers the first half of PCI Unit 1 (part a). It starts with the documents that every pharmaceutical plant must keep, then follows a generic medicine from idea to approval and beyond: the US law that created the generic route (Hatch-Waxman), the Code of Federal Regulations, how product performance is shown in vitro and in vivo, the ANDA and NDA processes, changes after scale-up, post-marketing surveillance, and how bioavailability (BA) and bioequivalence (BE) work is outsourced to contract research organisations (CROs).

The USA is used as the model because the syllabus and the reference books follow the FDA system. Indian equivalents are given where they matter. Numbers below (exclusivity periods, reporting days) were checked against FDA sources and the Code of Federal Regulations; regulations change, so in real work always read the current text on fda.gov, ecfr.gov or cdsco.gov.in.

## 1.1 Why documentation matters

A regulator cannot stand in a factory every day. It judges quality from records. The GMP principle is simple: **"if it is not written down, it was not done."** Good documentation:

1. Defines what must be done (specifications, master formula, SOPs).
2. Proves what was actually done for each batch (batch records, logbooks, test reports).
3. Allows any batch to be traced from raw material to patient (and back again in a recall).
4. Supports investigations of deviations, complaints and out-of-specification results.
5. Forms the evidence submitted in dossiers and checked during inspections.

Good documentation practice is often summarised as **ALCOA+**: records must be Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original and Accurate, plus Complete, Consistent, Enduring and Available. In India the documentation requirements are part of Schedule M of the Drugs Rules, 1945 (revised Schedule M notified in 2023); in the USA they are in 21 CFR Part 211 (cGMP for finished pharmaceuticals).

### Hierarchy of GMP documents

```text
            Quality manual / Site Master File
                        │
     Specifications ── Master Formula Record ── SOPs
                        │
       Batch Manufacturing Record / Batch Packaging Record
                        │
   Logbooks, test records, CoA, distribution records, reports
```

## 1.2 Master Formula Record (MFR)

**Definition:** the MFR (also called master production record or master manufacturing instruction) is the approved master document that states, for one product and one batch size, the complete formula and the full manufacturing and packaging instructions. Every batch manufacturing record (BMR) is a copy of the MFR filled in during production.

### Contents of an MFR

| Part | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Product identity | Name, strength, dosage form, product code, batch size, shelf life, storage |
| Preparation and approval | Prepared, checked and approved by named, qualified persons with dates; version number |
| Formula | Each ingredient by name and reference code, quantity per unit and per batch, including overages with justification; grade (IP/BP/USP) |
| Equipment | List of equipment and its size or type; line clearance requirements |
| Process instructions | Step-by-step method: dispensing, sieving, mixing times and speeds, granulation, drying temperature and end-point, compression or filling parameters, coating |
| In-process controls | Tests, limits and frequency (weight variation, hardness, LOD, pH, fill volume) |
| Yield | Theoretical yield and acceptable limits at stated stages |
| Packaging | Packaging materials with codes and quantities, packaging instructions, specimen of printed materials, batch coding |
| Precautions | Safety, environmental conditions, special handling (light, moisture) |
| Sampling and release | Samples to QC; final release requirements |

**Uses:** keeps every batch the same; is the basis of process validation; is referenced in the dossier (Module 3.2.P.3) and is one of the first documents an inspector asks for.

## 1.3 Drug Master File (DMF)

**Definition:** a DMF is a confidential, detailed document that a manufacturer submits to a regulator about the facilities, processes or materials used in making a drug component (usually the active pharmaceutical ingredient, API). It lets the supplier keep its know-how secret from its customers while the regulator can still review it.

### How it works (US system)

```text
API maker (DMF holder) ─ files DMF ─→ FDA (DMF number)
        │
        └─ Letter of Authorisation (LoA) ─→ finished product company
                                              │
                                              └─ cites DMF number + LoA
                                                 in its ANDA/NDA → FDA
                                                 reviews DMF with the application
```

- The FDA does **not approve or disapprove** a DMF on its own; it reviews it when an application refers to it. Deficiencies are sent to the holder, not to the applicant.
- The holder keeps it current with amendments and annual updates.
- For generic APIs, a DMF fee and a "completeness assessment" apply under the generic drug user-fee programme (GDUFA).

| Type | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Type I | Manufacturing site, facilities, procedures and personnel — no longer accepted |
| Type II | Drug substance, intermediate and materials used in their preparation, or drug product |
| Type III | Packaging material |
| Type IV | Excipient, colourant, flavour, essence or materials used in their preparation |
| Type V | FDA-accepted reference information (for example sterile manufacturing site data) |

A Type II DMF is now written in CTD format (mainly Module 3.2.S). Equivalent systems elsewhere: the EU **Active Substance Master File** (ASMF, with an applicant's part and a restricted part) or a **Certificate of Suitability (CEP)** from the EDQM; master file procedures in Canada, Japan and WHO prequalification.

## 1.4 Distribution records

**Definition:** records showing where each batch of a product was sent, so that it can be traced and recalled quickly.

- **Contents:** product name and strength, batch number, quantity, date of dispatch, name and address of consignee, mode of transport and invoice number, and (for cold-chain products) temperature records.
- **Purpose:** rapid and complete **recall**; handling complaints; checking returns; preventing diversion and counterfeits.
- **Retention:** kept at least as long as the law requires (in the USA, 21 CFR 211.196 links distribution records to the expiry date; in India Schedule M sets the period — check the current text).

Recall classes (FDA): **Class I** (reasonable probability of serious harm or death), **Class II** (temporary or reversible harm), **Class III** (unlikely to cause harm). Distribution records decide how deep a recall goes: to wholesaler, retailer or patient level.

## 1.5 Generic drug product development: introduction

A **generic drug** is a copy of an innovator (brand) product whose patents and exclusivities have expired or been challenged. To be approved it must be **pharmaceutically equivalent** (same active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route) and **bioequivalent** to the reference product. Pharmaceutical equivalence plus bioequivalence gives **therapeutic equivalence**, which the FDA lists in the Orange Book with "A" codes (for example AB).

### Stages of generic development

```text
Product selection (market, patents, exclusivity, technical difficulty)
 → Reference product characterisation (reverse engineering: composition,
   particle size, polymorph, dissolution in several media, impurities)
 → API sourcing (DMF holder, LoA) and excipient selection
 → Pre-formulation and formulation development (QbD: QTPP, CQAs, DoE)
 → Pilot BE study (often) → process optimisation and scale-up
 → Exhibit batch (pivotal) + stability + pivotal BE study
 → ANDA (CTD) filing → review, inspection → approval → launch
```

Key terms from ICH Q8 used in generic development: **QTPP** (quality target product profile — what the product must be), **CQA** (critical quality attributes such as assay, dissolution, impurities), **CPP** (critical process parameters) and the **design space**.

### Patent and exclusivity check

Before starting, the company reads the **Orange Book** ("Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations"), which lists approved drugs, their patents and exclusivity periods. Patent strategy decides whether the generic waits for expiry or files a Paragraph IV challenge.

## 1.6 Hatch-Waxman Act and amendments

The **Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act, 1984**, known as the **Hatch-Waxman Act**, amended the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act. It was a bargain between generic companies and innovators.

| For generic companies | For innovators |
| --- | --- |
| ANDA route under section 505(j): no repeat of safety and efficacy trials; BE to the reference listed drug (RLD) is enough | **Patent term restoration** for time lost in FDA review (patent term extension) |
| "Safe harbour": using a patented drug to develop data for FDA submission is not infringement | Data exclusivity periods during which generics cannot be approved (or filed) |
| 180-day exclusivity for the first applicant to file a successful Paragraph IV challenge | Patent listing in the Orange Book and an automatic **30-month stay** when they sue a Paragraph IV filer in time |

### Exclusivity periods (FDA)

| Exclusivity | Length |
| --- | --- |
| New chemical entity (NCE) | 5 years |
| New clinical investigation (new indication, dosage form etc. needing new clinical studies) | 3 years |
| Orphan drug | 7 years |
| Paediatric | 6 months added to existing patents and exclusivities |
| 180-day patent challenge (generic) | 180 days |
| Competitive generic therapy (generic) | 180 days |
| GAIN (qualifying infectious disease products) | 5 years added to certain exclusivities |

A US patent normally runs 20 years from the filing date of the application. During NCE exclusivity an ANDA with a Paragraph IV certification may be submitted only after four years (the "NCE-1" date); the exact statutory rules are in section 505(j)(5) of the FD&C Act.

### Patent certifications in an ANDA

| Certification | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Paragraph I | No patent information filed |
| Paragraph II | Patent has expired |
| Paragraph III | Patent will expire on a stated date; approval after that date |
| Paragraph IV | Patent is invalid or will not be infringed; notice to patent owner; suit within 45 days triggers the 30-month stay |
| Section viii statement | A patented method of use is "carved out" of the generic label |

### Later amendments that changed the scheme

| Law | Main change for generics |
| --- | --- |
| Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement and Modernization Act (MMA), 2003 | Limited the innovator to one 30-month stay per ANDA; introduced forfeiture events for the 180-day exclusivity; declaratory judgement actions |
| FDA Amendments Act (FDAAA), 2007 | Rules on citizen petitions (section 505(q)) that delay generics; REMS |
| FDA Safety and Innovation Act (FDASIA), 2012 | Created the **Generic Drug User Fee Amendments (GDUFA)**: fees in return for review goals and inspections |
| FDA Reauthorization Act (FDARA), 2017 | Competitive generic therapy designation with 180-day exclusivity; GDUFA II |
| Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act, 2009 | The biological counterpart: abbreviated route for biosimilars under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act |

## 1.7 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)

The **CFR** is the codification of the permanent rules published in the **Federal Register** by US federal agencies. It has 50 **titles**; **Title 21** covers Food and Drugs and is mostly FDA rules. A citation such as **21 CFR 314.94** means Title 21, Part 314, Section 94. The Federal Register is the daily publication where proposed and final rules first appear; the electronic CFR (eCFR) is updated continuously.

| Part (Title 21) | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 11 | Electronic records and electronic signatures |
| 50 | Protection of human subjects (informed consent) |
| 54 | Financial disclosure by clinical investigators |
| 56 | Institutional review boards |
| 58 | Good laboratory practice for non-clinical studies |
| 201 | Labelling |
| 210, 211 | cGMP (general; finished pharmaceuticals) |
| 312 | Investigational new drug application |
| 314 | Applications for FDA approval to market a new drug (NDA, ANDA) |
| 320 | Bioavailability and bioequivalence requirements |
| 600–680 | Biologics |
| 800 onwards | Medical devices (for example 807 for 510(k), 814 for PMA, 820 quality system) |

## 1.8 Drug product performance: in vitro

**Drug product performance** means the release of the drug from the dosage form leading to systemic availability. In vitro it is measured by **dissolution testing**.

1. **Dissolution method development:** apparatus (USP I basket, II paddle, IV flow-through), medium (pH 1.2, 4.5, 6.8, with surfactant if needed), volume, rotation speed, sampling times; must be discriminating (able to detect meaningful formulation changes).
2. **Comparison with the reference product:** profiles compared at several pH values. The **similarity factor f2** is used; **f2 between 50 and 100** means the profiles are similar (a mean difference of not more than 10% at each point).

```text
f2 = 50 × log { [1 + (1/n) Σ (Rt − Tt)²]^(−0.5) × 100 }
R, T = % dissolved of reference and test at time t; n = number of points
```

3. **Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS):** Class I high solubility–high permeability; II low–high; III high–low; IV low–low. For immediate-release products, a **BCS-based biowaiver** may replace an in vivo BE study for Class I (and, with stricter conditions, Class III) drugs, as set out in ICH M9.
4. **IVIVC (in vitro–in vivo correlation):** Level A (point-to-point) is the most useful; it can justify waivers for some changes of modified-release products.
5. **Biowaivers for lower strengths:** where the strengths are proportional in composition and dissolution is similar, BE on one strength may support the others.

## 1.9 Bioequivalence and drug product assessment: in vivo

**Bioavailability (BA):** the rate and extent to which the active ingredient is absorbed and becomes available at the site of action. **Bioequivalence (BE):** absence of a significant difference in the rate and extent of availability of two pharmaceutically equivalent products given at the same molar dose under similar conditions (21 CFR 320).

### Typical BE study design

| Element | Usual choice |
| --- | --- |
| Design | Randomised, two-period, two-sequence, crossover, single dose; washout ≥ 5 elimination half-lives |
| Subjects | Healthy adult volunteers (patients for toxic drugs such as many anticancer agents); number from a power calculation |
| Conditions | Fasting; fed study also for many products (as the product-specific guidance requires) |
| Sampling | Enough points to define Cmax and to cover at least 80% of AUC |
| Bioanalysis | Validated method (ICH M10) |
| Parameters | Cmax (rate), AUC0–t and AUC0–∞ (extent), Tmax |
| Statistics | Log-transformed data; ANOVA; **90% confidence interval of the test/reference ratio within 80.00–125.00%** for Cmax and AUC |

Special cases: highly variable drugs (reference-scaled average BE), narrow therapeutic index drugs (tighter limits in some regulators), replicate designs, steady-state studies, and clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic studies when blood levels cannot be measured (for example locally acting products). The FDA publishes **product-specific guidances** describing the BE study expected for each drug.

**Drug product assessment** in the ANDA brings together: pharmaceutical equivalence, BE, CMC quality, stability, labelling sameness and GMP of all sites.

## 1.10 ANDA regulatory approval process

```text
ANDA in eCTD (Module 1 to 5; Modules 4 and 5 mainly BE)
 → Filing review / receipt (completeness, fees paid, DMF complete)
      → "refuse to receive" if seriously incomplete
 → Discipline reviews: bioequivalence, chemistry/manufacturing
   (drug substance via DMF, drug product), microbiology (sterile),
   labelling (same as RLD)
 → Pre-approval inspections of manufacturing and testing sites,
   and of the BE clinical and analytical sites
 → Information requests / discipline review letters
 → Action: APPROVAL, TENTATIVE APPROVAL (blocked only by patent or
   exclusivity) or COMPLETE RESPONSE LETTER
```

Review is done by the **Office of Generic Drugs** (OGD) in CDER. Review goals are agreed under GDUFA; check the current commitment letter for exact months. ANDA requirements are in **21 CFR 314.94**.

## 1.11 NDA approval process (overview)

An **NDA** (21 CFR 314; form FDA 356h) asks for approval of a new drug and must prove safety and efficacy with full non-clinical and clinical data.

```text
Pre-IND meeting → IND → Phase I–III → end-of-Phase-II meeting
 → pre-NDA meeting → NDA submission (eCTD)
 → filing decision within 60 days ("refuse to file" possible)
 → review (medical, statistics, clinical pharmacology, pharm/tox,
   CMC, microbiology), advisory committee if needed,
   pre-approval inspection, labelling negotiation
 → approval letter or complete response letter
```

Review goals under PDUFA: **standard 10 months, priority 6 months** (for new molecular entities, counted from the 60-day filing date). Routes: 505(b)(1) full NDA; 505(b)(2) NDA relying partly on literature or FDA's earlier findings (new salt, new dosage form, new combination). Details are in Units 2 and 4.

## 1.12 Scale-up and post-approval changes (SUPAC)

Generic exhibit batches are often smaller than commercial batches. After approval, firms scale up, move sites, change equipment or suppliers. The FDA **SUPAC** guidances (SUPAC-IR for immediate-release solid oral forms, SUPAC-MR for modified release, SUPAC-SS for semisolids) classify such changes into levels by their likely effect on quality and performance.

| Level | Likely effect | Typical filing | Data usually needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Unlikely to have a detectable effect | Annual report | Application or compendial tests, stability on one batch in the annual report |
| 2 | Could have a significant effect | Changes-being-effected supplement (CBE-30) or prior approval supplement, depending on change | Multi-point dissolution comparison, stability |
| 3 | Likely to have a significant effect | Prior approval supplement | Dissolution, stability, and often an in vivo BE study |

Change types covered: **components and composition**, **site of manufacture**, **batch size (scale-up or scale-down)**, **manufacturing equipment** and **manufacturing process**. For SUPAC-IR a batch-size change of more than ten times the pilot or bio-batch is Level 2. The general rule for reporting categories is 21 CFR 314.70 (NDA) and 314.97 (ANDA): prior approval supplement for major changes, CBE-30 or CBE-0 for moderate, annual report for minor.

## 1.13 Post-marketing surveillance (PMS)

Clinical trials are too small and too short to find rare or delayed adverse reactions, so safety monitoring continues after approval.

**US requirements (21 CFR 314.80, applies to NDA and, via 314.98, ANDA holders):**

| Report | Timing |
| --- | --- |
| 15-day "alert report" | Each serious and unexpected adverse drug experience, within **15 calendar days** of first receipt; follow-ups within 15 days of new information |
| Periodic report | **Quarterly for 3 years** from approval (due within 30 days of the close of each quarter), then **annually** (within 60 days of the approval anniversary) |
| Records | Kept for **10 years** |

Other tools: FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and **MedWatch** (voluntary reporting by health professionals and patients); **Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS)** for high-risk drugs; post-marketing requirements and commitments (Phase IV studies); the Sentinel system for active surveillance using health-care data.

**India:** periodic safety update reports every six months for the first two years after approval and annually for the next two years (NDCT Rules, 2019); spontaneous reporting through the **Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)**, coordinated by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.

## 1.14 Outsourcing BA and BE studies to CROs

Most generic companies do not run their own clinical units; they contract **CROs** (contract research organisations) that have clinical facilities, bioanalytical laboratories and biostatistics teams.

### Steps in outsourcing

```text
Need identified (pilot or pivotal BE) → shortlist CROs
 → confidentiality agreement → request for proposal → technical and
   cost evaluation → qualification audit (facility, GCP, GLP,
   regulatory inspection history, data integrity, SOPs)
 → contract + quality agreement (who does what, data ownership,
   audit rights, timelines, subcontracting rules)
 → protocol finalised → ethics committee and regulator approvals
 → study conduct with sponsor monitoring → bioanalysis → statistics
 → clinical study report → sponsor audit → dossier
```

### Points to consider when choosing a CRO

1. Inspection history with the target regulators (FDA, EMA, MHRA, WHO, CDSCO); any untitled letters or warning letters.
2. Registration with the national authority (in India, BA/BE study centres need registration with the Central Licensing Authority under the NDCT Rules, 2019 — check the current rule) and a registered ethics committee.
3. Validated bioanalytical methods (ICH M10), calibrated instruments, LIMS and audit trails (21 CFR Part 11).
4. Volunteer database and safeguards against over-volunteering.
5. Quality assurance unit independent of operations; archiving of samples and data.

**Sponsor remains responsible:** under ICH E6, duties can be transferred to a CRO, but the sponsor stays ultimately responsible for the quality and integrity of the trial data. Regulators have rejected BE data from CROs with data integrity failures, which shows why audits matter.

## Remember

- Documents: quality manual → specifications, MFR, SOPs → BMR/BPR → records. ALCOA+. MFR = master; BMR = copy filled for each batch.
- DMF: confidential; LoA; FDA neither approves nor disapproves; Types II (API), III (packaging), IV (excipient), V (reference); Type I no longer used. EU: ASMF, CEP.
- Distribution records: batch-wise consignees for recall; FDA recall Classes I–III.
- Hatch-Waxman 1984: ANDA 505(j), patent term restoration, safe harbour, Paragraph I–IV, 30-month stay, 180-day exclusivity. NCE 5 y, new clinical investigation 3 y, orphan 7 y, paediatric 6 months.
- Amendments: MMA 2003, FDAAA 2007, FDASIA/GDUFA 2012, FDARA 2017 (CGT 180 days); BPCI Act 2009 for biosimilars.
- CFR Title 21: 11, 50, 56, 58, 211, 312, 314, 320; Federal Register publishes rules.
- In vitro: discriminating dissolution, f2 50–100, BCS biowaiver (ICH M9), IVIVC Level A.
- In vivo BE: crossover, Cmax and AUC, 90% CI 80.00–125.00%.
- ANDA: 21 CFR 314.94; OGD; tentative approval. NDA: 60-day filing, 10/6 months review.
- SUPAC Levels 1–3; 314.70: PAS, CBE-30, CBE-0, annual report.
- PMS (314.80): 15-day alert reports; quarterly 3 years then annual; records 10 years. India: PSUR 6-monthly × 2 y, yearly × 2 y; PvPI.
- CRO outsourcing: audit, contract, quality agreement; sponsor stays responsible.

# Unit 2: Regulatory requirements for product approval (USA as the model)

This unit covers the second half of PCI Unit 1 (part b): what a regulator needs before it approves an **active pharmaceutical ingredient (API)**, a **biological product** or a **novel therapy**, how an **NDA** and an **ANDA** are obtained, and the "ways and means" by which a company outside the USA (for example an Indian firm) gets its products onto the US market. Indian requirements are added where students are usually asked to compare.

US figures here were checked against FDA pages and Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations; rules and fees change every year, so always confirm on fda.gov before using them at work.

## 2.1 The US regulatory framework in one view

```text
Congress → Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act, 1938, amended)
         → Public Health Service Act (PHS Act) — biologics
FDA (under the Department of Health and Human Services)
   ├── CDER: drugs (NDA, ANDA, OTC), most therapeutic proteins and antibodies
   ├── CBER: vaccines, blood, cell and gene therapies, tissues
   ├── CDRH: medical devices
   └── Office of Combination Products (assigns lead centre)
Rules: Title 21 CFR; guidance documents (non-binding, show FDA's current thinking)
User fees: PDUFA (new drugs, biologics), GDUFA (generics), BsUFA (biosimilars),
           MDUFA (devices) — fees in exchange for agreed review goals
```

The key legal milestones: 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act; 1938 FD&C Act (safety, after the sulfanilamide elixir deaths); 1962 Kefauver–Harris Amendments (proof of efficacy, after thalidomide); 1983 Orphan Drug Act; 1984 Hatch-Waxman Act; 1992 PDUFA; 2009 BPCI Act; 2012 FDASIA; 2016 21st Century Cures Act.

## 2.2 Regulatory requirements for APIs

In the USA an API is **not approved on its own**. Its quality is reviewed as part of each drug application that uses it, usually through a **Type II DMF**. Requirements that an API maker must meet:

| Requirement | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| GMP for APIs | **ICH Q7** (Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients), adopted by FDA, EU, India and many others; applies from the introduction of the "API starting material" onwards |
| Establishment registration and drug listing | Every domestic and foreign site that makes, repacks or relabels drugs for the US market registers with FDA and lists its products (21 CFR Part 207) |
| DMF | Detailed CMC information (route of synthesis, controls, impurities, stability) filed in CTD Module 3.2.S, cited by customers through a Letter of Authorisation |
| Impurity control | ICH Q3A (organic impurities), Q3C (residual solvents), Q3D (elemental impurities), M7 (mutagenic impurities, including nitrosamines) |
| Stability | ICH Q1A(R2) conditions and retest period |
| Inspection | Pre-approval and routine surveillance inspections; foreign sites are inspected too |
| Fees | Generic API DMFs pay a GDUFA DMF fee; API facilities pay a facility fee |

**EU:** the API is described in an ASMF or covered by a **CEP** issued by the EDQM after assessment against the European Pharmacopoeia monograph; non-EU API makers need a "written confirmation" from their own regulator that their GMP is equivalent (EU Directive on falsified medicines).

**India:** API manufacture needs a licence from the State Licensing Authority under the Drugs Rules, 1945 and compliance with Schedule M; a **new** API (bulk drug not yet approved in India) needs permission of the Central Licensing Authority under the NDCT Rules, 2019.

## 2.3 Regulatory requirements for biologics

A **biological product** is a virus, therapeutic serum, toxin, antitoxin, vaccine, blood or blood component, allergenic product, protein or analogous product used to prevent, treat or cure a disease. Biologics are large, complex, made in living systems and sensitive to small process changes, so "the process is the product".

### Biologics License Application (BLA)

| Point | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Law | Section **351(a)** of the PHS Act; regulations 21 CFR Parts 600–680 (plus 210/211 and 312) |
| Standard | The product must be **safe, pure and potent**, and the facility must meet standards that assure this |
| Form | FDA 356h (same form as NDA) |
| Centre | CBER (vaccines, blood, cell and gene therapy) or CDER (most monoclonal antibodies and therapeutic proteins) |
| Extra elements | Detailed description of cell bank, viral safety, process validation, comparability protocols, lot release (some products need FDA lot release), establishment description |
| Outcome | A **biologics licence** (US licence number on the label) |

### Biosimilars and interchangeables

- Created by the **Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act (BPCI Act), 2009**; abbreviated route under section **351(k)** of the PHS Act.
- **Biosimilar:** highly similar to an FDA-licensed reference product (licensed under 351(a)), notwithstanding minor differences in clinically inactive components, with **no clinically meaningful differences** in safety, purity and potency.
- **Interchangeable:** a biosimilar that also meets extra standards so it may be substituted at the pharmacy without the prescriber's intervention (subject to state law).
- Evidence follows a "**totality of evidence**", stepwise approach: analytical comparability (structure, function) is the foundation, then animal data if needed, clinical pharmacology (PK/PD), immunogenicity and any comparative clinical study needed to resolve remaining uncertainty.
- The reference product has **12 years** of exclusivity from first licensure, during which a 351(k) application cannot be approved.
- The **Purple Book** lists licensed biological products with their biosimilar or interchangeable status and exclusivity dates (the biologic equivalent of the Orange Book).

**India:** biologics and similar biologics are approved by CDSCO (as new drugs under the NDCT Rules, 2019), with the **Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM)** of the Department of Biotechnology reviewing pre-clinical data for recombinant products, and the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** where living modified organisms are involved. The "Guidelines on Similar Biologics" set the comparability exercise; check the latest revision on cdsco.gov.in.

**EU:** biotechnology products must use the centralised procedure (EMA). The EU approved the first biosimilar in 2006 and has detailed product-class guidelines.

## 2.4 Regulatory requirements for novel therapies

"Novel therapies" include new molecular entities, **cell and gene therapies**, tissue-engineered products, RNA-based medicines, and therapies for rare diseases.

### US programmes that speed up development and review

| Programme | Qualifying criteria | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fast track** | Serious condition + potential to meet an unmet medical need (non-clinical or clinical data) | More frequent meetings; **rolling review** (sections submitted as completed) |
| **Breakthrough therapy** | Serious condition + preliminary clinical evidence of substantial improvement on a clinically significant endpoint | All fast-track features + intensive guidance from senior FDA staff |
| **Accelerated approval** | Serious condition, meaningful advantage, effect on a **surrogate endpoint** reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit | Earlier approval; **confirmatory trial** required |
| **Priority review** | Significant improvement in safety or effectiveness for a serious condition | Review goal 6 months instead of 10 |
| **RMAT** (regenerative medicine advanced therapy, 21st Century Cures Act 2016) | Cell therapy, tissue product or certain gene therapies for serious conditions, with preliminary clinical evidence | Breakthrough-like benefits |
| **Orphan drug designation** (Orphan Drug Act 1983) | Disease affecting fewer than 200,000 people in the USA (or no expected cost recovery) | 7-year orphan exclusivity, tax credits, fee waivers |

### Special regulatory points for cell and gene therapies

- Regulated by CBER's Office of Therapeutic Products; filed as INDs then BLAs.
- Long-term follow-up of patients (for some gene therapies, many years) for delayed effects.
- Vector shedding, replication-competent virus testing, potency assays that reflect the mechanism.
- Chain of identity and chain of custody for autologous products.
- Manufacturing comparability when the process changes.

**EU:** advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) go through the centralised procedure with the **Committee for Advanced Therapies (CAT)**; the EU also has **PRIME** (priority medicines) support and conditional marketing authorisation.

**India:** the NDCT Rules, 2019 treat products such as recombinant DNA products, monoclonal antibodies, stem-cell-derived products and gene therapy products as **new drugs** needing CLA permission; trials of such products need appropriate ethics committee and, where relevant, DBT committee review. There is also a provision to waive local trials for drugs approved in specified countries in some situations (orphan drugs, unmet need) — check the current rule and notifications before quoting it.

## 2.5 Obtaining an NDA

### a. Legal routes

| Route | Use | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 505(b)(1) | New molecular entity or any product where the applicant owns or has right of reference to all studies | Full non-clinical and clinical package |
| 505(b)(2) | Changes to an approved drug (new salt, ester, dosage form, strength, route, combination, indication) or a new drug relying partly on literature or FDA's earlier findings | Bridging studies + new studies needed for the change; patent certifications for relied-upon drugs |

### b. Steps

```text
1. Pre-IND meeting → IND (21 CFR 312) → Phase I–III trials
2. Formal meetings with FDA:
     Type A (to resolve a stalled programme),
     Type B (pre-IND, end-of-Phase-II, pre-NDA),
     Type C (other topics) — plus newer types for specific needs
3. NDA in eCTD: Form FDA 356h, user fee (PDUFA), Modules 1–5,
   patent information, financial disclosure (21 CFR 54),
   debarment certification, proposed labelling (PLR format)
4. Filing review — 60 days ("refuse to file" if not reviewable)
5. Day-74 letter: filing communication and review designation
6. Review by disciplines; mid-cycle and late-cycle meetings;
   advisory committee if questions of benefit–risk remain
7. Pre-approval inspections (manufacturing, clinical sites — BIMO)
8. Labelling negotiation; REMS if needed
9. Action: approval letter or complete response letter
10. Post-approval: Phase IV commitments, safety reports, annual reports,
    supplements for changes
```

### c. Labelling

The US prescribing information follows the **Physician Labeling Rule (PLR)** format with "Highlights", a table of contents and the full prescribing information. Patient labelling (Medication Guide, patient package insert) may also be required. The approved label becomes the reference that generics must copy.

## 2.6 ANDA for generic drugs (requirements recap)

An ANDA (section 505(j); 21 CFR 314.94) must show:

1. The **reference listed drug (RLD)** it copies and the **reference standard** used for BE.
2. Same active ingredient, route, dosage form, strength and conditions of use.
3. Labelling the same as the RLD (except permitted differences).
4. **Bioequivalence** (or a justified biowaiver), following the FDA product-specific guidance.
5. Full CMC: drug substance (usually via DMF), drug product composition, pharmaceutical development, manufacturing process, specifications, container closure, **stability** (exhibit batches), and inactive ingredients justified for the route (the FDA Inactive Ingredient Database is checked for acceptable levels).
6. **Patent certifications** and exclusivity statements.
7. Facility information and GMP compliance; GDUFA fees paid.

Complex generics (inhalers, injectables with complex release, topical products, peptides) may need extra studies (in vitro characterisation, comparative clinical endpoint studies, immunogenicity risk assessment). **Pre-ANDA meetings** help resolve such issues before filing.

## 2.7 Ways and means of US registration for foreign drugs

An Indian company can supply the US market in three main ways: by filing its **own ANDA or NDA**, by being the **API/DMF supplier** to a US applicant, or as a **contract manufacturer** named in someone else's application. In every case the steps below apply.

### a. Steps for a foreign firm

```text
1. Obtain a DUNS number (unique business identifier used by FDA)
2. Establishment registration of each foreign site (21 CFR 207),
   naming a US agent; renewed every year; drug listing with NDC codes
3. Appoint a US agent (and usually a US regulatory consultant /
   authorised representative for correspondence)
4. Prepare dossier: ANDA/NDA in eCTD via the FDA electronic
   submissions gateway; DMF for the API
5. Pay user fees (application, facility, DMF fees as applicable)
6. FDA review → pre-approval inspection of the foreign site
   (FDA has overseas offices, including in India)
7. Approval → commercial batches → import into the USA:
   customs entry, FDA admissibility review, possible sampling
8. Post-approval: annual reports, safety reporting, supplements,
   surveillance inspections, product listing updates
```

### b. Key import controls

| Control | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Admissibility review | FDA checks each import entry (registration, listing, approval status, labelling) |
| Refusal of admission | Product refused if it appears adulterated, misbranded or unapproved |
| **Import alert** | Lets FDA detain shipments without physical examination ("detention without physical examination") from a firm with serious GMP problems |
| Form FDA 483 | List of observations given at the end of an inspection |
| Warning letter | Formal notice of significant violations; must be answered |
| Official Action Indicated (OAI) | Inspection classification that can block approvals from that site |

### c. Practical tips for Indian firms

1. Build data integrity into systems from the start (audit trails, Part 11 computer systems); many FDA warning letters to Indian sites concern data integrity.
2. Keep the site inspection-ready at all times; FDA may give short notice abroad.
3. Choose BE CROs with clean inspection histories.
4. Use the US reference product for BE and US-specific labelling.
5. Track US patents and exclusivities to plan Paragraph IV or launch timing.

## 2.8 India: approval of new drugs (for comparison)

| Step | Under the NDCT Rules, 2019 |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical trial permission | Application in Form CT-04; permission in Form CT-06; ethics committee approval and CTRI registration also needed |
| Import of a new drug for sale | Application in Form CT-18 |
| Manufacture of a new drug for sale | Application in Form CT-21 |
| Review | CDSCO with the Subject Expert Committee (SEC) |
| Timelines | Clinical trial application decided within 90 working days; 30 working days for a drug discovered and developed in India (deemed approval if not answered) |
| After approval | State manufacturing licence; PSURs every six months for two years, then yearly for two years |

Applications are submitted online through CDSCO's **SUGAM** portal. The dossier follows the CTD format.

## 2.9 Comparison: NDA, ANDA, BLA and 351(k)

| Point | NDA 505(b)(1) | 505(b)(2) | ANDA 505(j) | BLA 351(a) | Biosimilar 351(k) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product | New drug | Modified drug | Generic | New biologic | Biosimilar |
| Law | FD&C Act | FD&C Act | FD&C Act | PHS Act | PHS Act |
| Clinical efficacy trials | Yes | Only as needed | No | Yes | Usually limited/comparative |
| Key evidence | Safety and efficacy | Bridging + new data | BE | Safe, pure, potent | Analytical similarity + PK/PD + immunogenicity |
| Reference list | Orange Book | Orange Book | Orange Book | Purple Book | Purple Book |
| Exclusivity | NCE 5 y; 3 y | 3 y possible | 180-day, CGT | 12 y reference product | First interchangeable exclusivity |

## Remember

- APIs: no stand-alone US approval; ICH Q7 GMP; DMF Type II; registration and listing (21 CFR 207); impurities Q3A/Q3C/Q3D/M7. EU: ASMF/CEP + written confirmation. India: SLA licence; new API needs CLA.
- Biologics: BLA 351(a), 21 CFR 600–680, "safe, pure and potent"; CBER/CDER. Biosimilar 351(k), BPCI Act 2009; interchangeable; 12-year reference exclusivity; Purple Book. India: CDSCO + RCGM + GEAC; similar biologics guidelines.
- Novel therapies: fast track, breakthrough, accelerated approval (surrogate + confirmatory trial), priority review (6 months), RMAT, orphan (< 200,000 patients; 7 years). EU: CAT, PRIME.
- NDA: 505(b)(1) vs 505(b)(2); Form 356h; meetings Type A/B/C; 60-day filing; PLR labelling; REMS.
- ANDA: RLD, sameness, BE, CMC, patent certification, GDUFA.
- Foreign registration: DUNS, establishment registration + listing with US agent, eCTD, fees, pre-approval inspection, import admissibility; Form 483, warning letter, import alert.
- India: CT-04 → CT-06; CT-18 import, CT-21 manufacture; 90/30 working days; SUGAM.
