# Unit 3: CMC, post-approval changes, combination products and devices, CTD/eCTD, ICH and other regulators

This unit is PCI Unit 2. It covers the **chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC)** part of a dossier, how products are changed after approval, how **combination products** and **medical devices** are regulated, the **CTD and eCTD** formats, how industry works with the FDA, the four families of **ICH guidelines**, and the regulators of the **EU, UK (MHRA), Australia (TGA)** and the "rest of the world" (ROW).

Figures in this unit were checked on fda.gov, ema.europa.eu, ich.org and cdsco.gov.in. Post-approval rules in the EU and UK were being revised around 2024–2025, so for real filings always read the current guideline.

## 3.1 Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC)

**CMC** is the part of a regulatory submission that describes what the product is made of, how it is made and how its quality is controlled. In the CTD it is **Module 3 (Quality)**, summarised in the **Quality Overall Summary (Module 2.3)**. Clinical data show a drug works; CMC shows that **every batch sold is the same as the batches that were tested**.

### a. Contents of Module 3 (ICH M4Q)

| Section | Drug substance (3.2.S) | Drug product (3.2.P) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General information | Nomenclature, structure, properties | Description and composition |
| Manufacture | Manufacturer, process description and flow chart, control of materials, critical steps and intermediates, process validation, manufacturing process development | Manufacturer, batch formula, process and controls, critical steps, process validation |
| Development | Covered under manufacturing development | **Pharmaceutical development (3.2.P.2)**: formulation and process development, overages, physicochemical and biological properties, container closure, microbiological attributes, compatibility |
| Characterisation | Proof of structure, impurities | — |
| Control | Specification, analytical procedures, validation, batch analyses, justification | Same for the finished product; control of excipients (3.2.P.4) |
| Reference standards | Yes | Yes |
| Container closure | Yes | Yes |
| Stability | Summary, post-approval protocol, data | Same |
| Appendices / regional | 3.2.A facilities and equipment, adventitious agent safety, novel excipients; 3.2.R regional information (for example executed batch records for FDA) | |

### b. Why CMC matters to regulatory affairs

1. CMC deficiencies are a frequent reason for complete response letters and delayed approvals.
2. Every later change (site, scale, supplier, specification) is judged against the approved CMC.
3. CMC links to GMP: inspectors check that the plant does what Module 3 says.
4. CMC data are built progressively: limited at Phase I (safety-related quality), fuller at Phase III, complete at NDA.

### c. Guidelines that drive CMC

ICH Q1 (stability), Q2 (validation of analytical procedures), Q3 (impurities), Q6A/Q6B (specifications), Q8 (pharmaceutical development), Q9 (quality risk management), Q10 (pharmaceutical quality system), Q11 (development and manufacture of drug substances), Q12 (product life-cycle management), Q13 (continuous manufacturing), Q14 (analytical procedure development).

## 3.2 Post-approval regulatory affairs

After approval the product has a long life: new sites, scale-up, new suppliers, specification changes, label updates, safety variations, renewals and eventually withdrawal. **Post-approval regulatory affairs** manages all of this so that the licence stays valid and every change is approved or notified correctly.

### a. Main post-approval activities

```text
Change control (internal) → regulatory assessment of each change
 → filing category decided → supplement / variation submitted
 → approval or acknowledgement → implementation → update of dossier
Parallel duties: safety reporting, periodic reports, annual reports,
labelling updates, renewals, responses to inspections, recalls,
product listing, maintenance of DMFs and certificates
```

### b. USA — changes to an approved application (21 CFR 314.70; 314.97 for ANDAs; 601.12 for biologics)

| Category | Filing | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Major change | **Prior Approval Supplement (PAS)** | Only after FDA approval |
| Moderate change | **CBE-30** (changes being effected in 30 days) | 30 days after FDA receives it, unless FDA objects |
| Moderate change (designated) | **CBE-0** | On receipt by FDA |
| Minor change | **Annual report** | At once; reported in the next annual report |

Examples: change in qualitative formula → PAS; new container closure not affecting quality → CBE-30; strengthening a warning → CBE-0; deleting a colouring agent used only for colour → annual report. ICH **Q12** adds tools such as **established conditions** and **post-approval change management protocols** that let a firm agree the reporting category of future changes in advance.

The **annual report** (21 CFR 314.81) is submitted within 60 days of the approval anniversary and includes distribution data, labelling, CMC changes, non-clinical and clinical study updates and the status of post-marketing commitments.

### c. European Union — variations

Variations to EU marketing authorisations are governed by the Variations Regulation (Commission Regulation (EC) No 1234/2008, as amended) and its classification guideline:

| Type | Meaning | How it is handled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type IA | Minimal or no impact | "Do and tell": implement, then notify (some must be notified immediately — Type IA-IN) |
| Type IB | Minor, not IA or II | "Tell, wait and do": implement if no objection within the set period |
| Type II | Major impact on quality, safety or efficacy (for example new indication) | Prior assessment and approval |
| Extension | Change to active substance, strength, dosage form or route | New application procedure |

Grouping and **work-sharing** allow one assessment of the same change across several products or authorisations. The EU updated its variations framework in 2024–2025; check the current guideline.

### d. India

Changes to an approved new drug (and to licensed products) are handled under the Drugs Rules, 1945 and the NDCT Rules, 2019, with CDSCO guidance on post-approval changes classifying them as major (prior approval) or minor (notification). Check the current CDSCO guidance before filing.

## 3.3 Regulation of combination products

**Definition (21 CFR 3.2(e)):** a combination product is made of two or more regulated components (drug, device, biological product) that are:

1. physically, chemically or otherwise combined into a **single entity** (for example a drug-eluting stent, a prefilled syringe, a transdermal patch with a device element);
2. **co-packaged** in one package (for example a kit with a drug and its delivery device);
3. a **separately packaged** product intended for use only with a specific approved product, where both are needed and the labelling must change (cross-labelled);
4. a separately packaged investigational product intended only for use with another specified investigational product.

### Primary mode of action (PMOA)

- **Mode of action:** how the product achieves its therapeutic effect — as a drug, a device or a biological product.
- **PMOA (21 CFR 3.2(m)):** the single mode of action that provides the **most important therapeutic action** of the combination product.
- The FDA **Office of Combination Products (OCP)** assigns the **lead centre** (CDER, CBER or CDRH) based on the PMOA. If the PMOA is uncertain, the sponsor can file a **Request for Designation (RFD)**.

| Example | PMOA | Lead centre |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug-eluting coronary stent | Device (keeps vessel open) | CDRH |
| Prefilled insulin pen | Drug | CDER |
| Antibody–drug conjugate | Biological | CDER (therapeutic biologic) |

**Applications:** usually one marketing application of the lead centre's type (NDA, BLA or PMA/510(k)) with consultation by the other centres. **GMP:** 21 CFR Part 4 lets the manufacturer follow one main GMP system (drug cGMP or device quality system) plus specified extra provisions from the other.

**EU:** a medicine with an integrated device is authorised as a medicine, but the device part must meet the general safety and performance requirements of the Medical Devices Regulation (a notified body opinion is needed in many cases). **India:** drug–device combinations are regulated as drugs or as devices depending on the primary purpose; check CDSCO's classification lists.

## 3.4 Regulation of medical devices

A **medical device** is an instrument, apparatus, implant, machine, software or similar article intended for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring or treatment, which achieves its main intended action **not** by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic means.

### a. USA (CDRH)

| Class | Risk | Controls | Usual pathway |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | Low (for example bandages, examination gloves) | General controls | Most exempt; otherwise 510(k) |
| II | Moderate (for example infusion pumps, powered wheelchairs) | General + special controls | **510(k) premarket notification** (substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate) |
| III | High (for example implantable pacemakers, heart valves) | General controls + premarket approval | **PMA** (premarket approval with clinical evidence) |

Other routes: **De Novo** classification for novel low-to-moderate risk devices with no predicate (classified into Class I or II); **Humanitarian Device Exemption (HDE)** for devices for rare conditions; **IDE** (investigational device exemption, 21 CFR 812) for clinical studies. Quality system requirements are in 21 CFR Part 820 (now aligned with ISO 13485).

### b. European Union

Medical Devices Regulation **(EU) 2017/745 (MDR)** and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation **(EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)**. Devices are classed **I, IIa, IIb and III** by risk. Except low-risk Class I, conformity is assessed by an independent **notified body**, after which the maker affixes the **CE mark**. Requirements include clinical evaluation, post-market surveillance, a unique device identifier (UDI) and registration in the EUDAMED database.

### c. India

The **Medical Devices Rules, 2017** (under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act) classify devices by risk into **Class A (lowest), B, C and D (highest)**.

| Licensing | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| Manufacture of Class A and B | State Licensing Authority |
| Manufacture of Class C and D | Central Licensing Authority (CDSCO) |
| Import of all classes | Central Licensing Authority |
| Non-sterile, non-measuring Class A | Exempt from licence; registration on the online portal |

CDSCO publishes class-wise lists that change over time; check the current list for a specific device.

## 3.5 CTD and eCTD

### a. Common Technical Document (ICH M4)

The CTD is the agreed **format** for organising a registration dossier. It harmonises format, not data requirements.

```text
                      /\
                     /M1\        Regional administrative information
                    /----\
                   /  M2  \      Summaries (QOS, overviews, written and
                  /--------\     tabulated summaries)
                 / M3 |M4 |M5\   Quality | Non-clinical | Clinical reports
                /-----+---+---\
```

| Module | Content |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Regional: forms, cover letter, fees, labelling, certificates, patent and exclusivity (USA), environmental risk (EU), Indian forms under NDCT Rules |
| 2 | 2.1 contents; 2.2 introduction; 2.3 Quality Overall Summary; 2.4 non-clinical overview; 2.5 clinical overview; 2.6 non-clinical summaries; 2.7 clinical summary |
| 3 | Quality (3.2.S, 3.2.P, 3.2.A, 3.2.R) |
| 4 | Non-clinical study reports (pharmacology, PK, toxicology) |
| 5 | Clinical study reports (BA/BE, PK, PD, efficacy and safety, post-marketing data, CRFs) |

Advantages: one core dossier reused worldwide; faster review; easier exchange between regulators; basis for electronic submissions.

### b. Electronic CTD (eCTD, ICH M8 / earlier M2 work)

| Feature | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Folder structure | m1 to m5 folders matching the modules |
| XML backbone | Index file listing every document, its location and life-cycle status |
| Documents | PDF with bookmarks and hyperlinks; some data sets in specified formats |
| Sequences | Each submission numbered 0000, 0001 … |
| Life-cycle operations | New, replace, append, delete |
| Checksums | Detect any change or corruption of files |
| Regional Module 1 | Each regulator publishes its own specification |
| Validation | Technical validation before review |

Version 3.2.2 has been used for many years; **eCTD v4.0** is being introduced by regulators step by step. The FDA requires eCTD for NDAs, ANDAs, BLAs, commercial INDs and master files (with stated exceptions); EU centralised applications are in eCTD; CDSCO accepts CTD dossiers through SUGAM (check its notices for electronic format requirements).

## 3.6 Industry and FDA liaison

Regulatory affairs (RA) professionals are the official link between a company and the regulator. Good liaison shortens development and avoids rejections.

### a. Channels of communication

| Channel | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Formal meetings (Type A, B, C and others) | Pre-IND, end-of-Phase-II, pre-NDA/BLA, resolving disputes |
| Written responses | Answers to information requests and discipline review letters |
| Special protocol assessment (SPA) | Agreement on design of pivotal trials, carcinogenicity studies or stability protocols |
| Advisory committee meetings | Public expert discussion of an application |
| Formal dispute resolution | Appeal above the review division |
| Small business and industry assistance (CDER SBIA), guidance documents, workshops | Education and clarification |
| Inspections and responses | Form 483 response within the expected time, CAPA, follow-up |
| Comment on draft guidance and proposed rules | Docket comments via the Federal Register |

### b. Role of RA in liaison

1. Plan the regulatory strategy and the meeting schedule.
2. Prepare briefing packages with precise questions.
3. Keep minutes and track every commitment.
4. Coordinate submissions with R&D, QA, manufacturing, clinical and legal.
5. Maintain honest, timely, documented communication — credibility with the regulator is a company asset.
6. Watch for new laws, guidances and enforcement trends (regulatory intelligence).

## 3.7 ICH guidelines: Q, S, E and M

The **International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH)** brings together regulators and industry to harmonise technical requirements. It began in 1990 (EU, USA, Japan) and became an international association in 2015; many regulators have since joined (for example Health Canada, Swissmedic, ANVISA Brazil, NMPA China and others). CDSCO India is an observer. Guidelines pass through a five-step process (Step 4 = adoption by ICH; Step 5 = implementation by each regulator).

### a. Quality (Q)

| Guideline | Topic |
| --- | --- |
| Q1A–Q1E | Stability testing (Q1B photostability) |
| Q2 | Validation of analytical procedures |
| Q3A–Q3D | Impurities in drug substances, products, residual solvents, elemental impurities |
| Q4B | Pharmacopoeial harmonisation |
| Q5A–Q5E | Quality of biotechnological products (viral safety, comparability Q5E) |
| Q6A, Q6B | Specifications |
| Q7 | GMP for APIs |
| Q8 | Pharmaceutical development (QbD) |
| Q9 | Quality risk management |
| Q10 | Pharmaceutical quality system |
| Q11 | Development and manufacture of drug substances |
| Q12 | Product life-cycle management |
| Q13 | Continuous manufacturing |
| Q14 | Analytical procedure development |

### b. Safety (S)

S1 carcinogenicity; S2 genotoxicity; S3 toxicokinetics; S4 duration of chronic toxicity studies; S5 reproductive toxicity; S6 pre-clinical safety of biotechnology products; S7A safety pharmacology and S7B QT (non-clinical); S8 immunotoxicity; S9 anticancer pharmaceuticals; S10 photosafety; S11 juvenile animal studies; S12 biodistribution for gene therapy products.

### c. Efficacy (E)

E1 extent of exposure for long-term treatment; E2A–E2F pharmacovigilance (E2A expedited reporting, E2B electronic case reports, E2C periodic benefit-risk evaluation report, E2D post-approval safety data, E2E pharmacovigilance planning, E2F development safety update report); E3 clinical study reports; E4 dose-response; E5 ethnic factors and bridging; **E6 Good Clinical Practice** (R3 adopted in 2025, with Annex 2 added later); E7 geriatrics; E8 general considerations; E9 statistical principles; E10 choice of control group; E11 paediatrics; E14 QT/QTc (clinical); E15–E16 pharmacogenomics and biomarkers; E17 multi-regional trials; E18 genomic sampling; E19 selective safety data collection.

### d. Multidisciplinary (M)

M1 MedDRA (medical dictionary for regulatory activities); M2 electronic standards; M3 non-clinical studies needed to support clinical trials; **M4 CTD**; M7 mutagenic impurities; **M8 eCTD**; M9 BCS-based biowaivers; M10 bioanalytical method validation; M11 structured clinical protocol; M12 drug interaction studies; M13 bioequivalence for immediate-release oral solid forms.

ICH adds and revises guidelines regularly; check the list and status on ich.org.

## 3.8 Regulatory requirements of the EU

- **EMA** (Amsterdam) coordinates scientific evaluation through committees: **CHMP** (opinions on human medicines), **PRAC** (pharmacovigilance), **CAT** (advanced therapies), **COMP** (orphans), **PDCO** (paediatrics), HMPC (herbal). The **European Commission** grants the binding authorisation; national competent authorities run national procedures.
- **Procedures:** centralised (compulsory for biotech products, ATMPs, orphan drugs and new substances for certain diseases; one EU-wide authorisation), decentralised, mutual recognition and national.
- **Centralised timeline:** CHMP evaluation up to **210 active days** (clock stops for questions), then Commission decision within **67 days** of the opinion.
- Validity five years, then renewal (usually unlimited after that).
- Requirements: **Qualified Person (QP)** batch release in the EU; **paediatric investigation plan (PIP)**; **risk management plan (RMP)**; pharmacovigilance system master file; GMP certificate of each site.
- Clinical trials under the **Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014**, applying since 31 January 2022 through CTIS (Unit 4).

## 3.9 Regulatory requirements of the UK (MHRA)

- **MHRA** (executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care) regulates medicines, devices and blood components; the **Commission on Human Medicines** advises.
- Since leaving the EU, the UK grants its own marketing authorisations. Routes include full national applications and reliance routes such as the **International Recognition Procedure**, which uses approvals of trusted reference regulators; the UK also joins the **Access Consortium** and **Project Orbis** (oncology) work-sharing.
- **Yellow Card** scheme for adverse reaction reporting; MHRA inspects GMP, GDP, GCP and GLP.
- The legal base is the Human Medicines Regulations 2012; Northern Ireland arrangements differ — check current MHRA guidance.

## 3.10 Regulatory requirements of Australia (TGA)

- **Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)**, part of the Department of Health, under the **Therapeutic Goods Act 1989**.
- Every therapeutic good must be on the **Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG)** before supply.

| Category | Risk | Label number |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered medicines (prescription, many OTC) | Higher; full evaluation | AUST R |
| Listed medicines (mainly complementary) | Low; permitted ingredients and claims only | AUST L |
| Medical devices | Classified by risk | ARTG entry |

- Prescription medicines are evaluated in CTD format with an Australian Module 1; pathways include standard, priority, provisional approval and work-sharing (Access Consortium with Canada, Singapore, Switzerland and the UK).
- Clinical trials run under the **CTN** (notification) or **CTA** (approval) scheme.

## 3.11 Rest of the world (ROW) markets

"ROW" usually means markets outside the USA, EU, UK, Japan, Canada and Australia: Asia, Africa, Latin America, the Middle East and the CIS. They matter greatly to Indian exporters.

| Region / body | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| ASEAN | **ACTD** (four parts: administrative, quality, non-clinical, clinical) with ACTR; national registration in each member state |
| Gulf Cooperation Council | Gulf centralised registration plus national registration; CTD with regional Module 1 |
| Africa | National authorities (for example SAHPRA in South Africa); regional harmonisation programmes; the African Medicines Agency is being set up |
| Latin America | ANVISA (Brazil), COFEPRIS (Mexico) and others; local BE and stability (climatic zone IV) often required |
| China, Japan | NMPA (China) and PMDA/MHLW (Japan) — ICH members using CTD with regional Module 1; Japan may need bridging data (ICH E5) |
| Eurasian Economic Union | Common rules for member states such as Russia |
| WHO prequalification | Assesses medicines for UN procurement (HIV, TB, malaria, vaccines); many African and Asian regulators rely on it |

Common ROW requirements: **Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (COPP)** in the WHO format from the exporting country's authority, free sale certificate, GMP certificate, local agent, labelling in the local language, stability for the local climatic zone, samples and reference standards, and sometimes local testing or inspection. Indian firms usually keep one core CTD and adapt Module 1 (or ACTD Part I) country by country.

## Remember

- CMC = Module 3 (3.2.S, 3.2.P, 3.2.A, 3.2.R) + QOS 2.3; shows every batch matches the tested batches.
- US post-approval: PAS, CBE-30, CBE-0, annual report (314.70/314.97/601.12; annual report 314.81 within 60 days of anniversary). ICH Q12 established conditions and PACMPs.
- EU variations: IA (do and tell), IB (tell, wait, do), II (prior approval), extension; work-sharing.
- Combination product: 4 types (21 CFR 3.2(e)); PMOA (3.2(m)) decides lead centre; OCP; RFD; Part 4 GMP.
- Devices: US Class I/II/III; 510(k), De Novo, PMA, HDE, IDE; Part 820. EU MDR 2017/745 (I, IIa, IIb, III; CE mark; notified body). India MDR 2017 Class A–D; SLA for A/B manufacture, CLA for C/D and all imports.
- CTD M4: five modules; M1 regional. eCTD: m1–m5, XML backbone, sequences, new/replace/append/delete, checksums; v3.2.2 → v4.0.
- FDA liaison: Type A/B/C meetings, SPA, advisory committees, dispute resolution, 483 responses.
- ICH: Q (Q1–Q14), S (S1–S12), E (E1–E19; E6 GCP R3 2025), M (M1 MedDRA, M4 CTD, M7, M8 eCTD, M9, M10, M13).
- EU: EMA committees; centralised 210 + 67 days; QP release; PIP; RMP. UK MHRA: IRP, Yellow Card. Australia TGA: ARTG, AUST R/L, CTN/CTA.
- ROW: ACTD, GCC, WHO PQ, COPP, climatic zone IV stability, local agent and labelling.

# Unit 4: Non-clinical drug development and global submissions

This unit is PCI Unit 3. It explains the **non-clinical (pre-clinical) studies** that must be done before and alongside human trials, how the first human dose is chosen, and how the resulting data are filed **globally**: the IND and its equivalents in other regions, then the NDA and ANDA (and their foreign counterparts). It ends with two documents named in the syllabus: the EU **Investigational Medicinal Product Dossier (IMPD)** and the **Investigator's Brochure (IB)**.

US items (IND contents, Investigator's Brochure contents) were checked against 21 CFR 312.23; EU clinical trial dates against the EMA website. Check the current texts before using them at work.

## 4.1 Drug development: where non-clinical work fits

```text
Target identification and validation
 → Hit → lead → lead optimisation → candidate selection
 → NON-CLINICAL DEVELOPMENT (pharmacology, ADME, toxicology, CMC)
 → IND / CTA → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III (non-clinical studies
   continue in parallel: chronic toxicity, reproductive, carcinogenicity)
 → NDA / MAA → approval → Phase IV
```

Only a small fraction of candidates that enter non-clinical development reach the market; development usually takes many years. Non-clinical studies aim to:

1. Identify the pharmacological effects and mechanism of action.
2. Characterise toxicity: target organs, dose dependence, reversibility.
3. Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME).
4. Choose a safe starting dose and a dose-escalation plan for humans.
5. Identify parameters to monitor clinically.
6. Support each later phase and the final marketing application.

## 4.2 Components of a non-clinical programme

### a. Pharmacology

| Study | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Primary pharmacodynamics | Effect on the intended target and disease models |
| Secondary pharmacodynamics | Effects on other targets (off-target) |
| **Safety pharmacology (ICH S7A)** | Effects on vital functions. **Core battery:** central nervous system, cardiovascular system and respiratory system |
| QT liability (ICH S7B with E14) | hERG channel assay and in vivo QT study to predict delayed ventricular repolarisation |
| Drug interactions (pharmacodynamic) | Where relevant |

### b. Pharmacokinetics and ADME

Absorption and bioavailability in test species; plasma protein binding; tissue distribution (including placental and milk transfer when needed); metabolism (in vitro with liver microsomes and hepatocytes from animals and humans; metabolite identification; CYP inhibition and induction, ICH M12); excretion and mass balance; **toxicokinetics (ICH S3A)** — exposure measured in toxicity studies so that animal exposure can be compared with human exposure.

### c. Toxicology

| Study | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Single-dose (acute) toxicity | Often as dose-range finding; information on overdose |
| Repeat-dose toxicity | In two species (one rodent, one non-rodent) for small molecules; duration matched to the clinical trial duration (ICH M3(R2)); chronic studies defined by ICH S4 |
| Genotoxicity (ICH S2) | Standard battery: bacterial reverse mutation (Ames) test + an in vitro mammalian cell test and/or in vivo test (for example micronucleus) |
| Carcinogenicity (ICH S1) | For drugs used long term or with cause for concern; usually completed before marketing |
| Reproductive and developmental toxicity (ICH S5) | Fertility, embryo-foetal development, pre- and post-natal development; timing tied to inclusion of women of child-bearing potential |
| Local tolerance | At the site of administration |
| Immunotoxicity (S8), phototoxicity (S10), juvenile animal studies (S11) | When indicated |
| Biotechnology products (ICH S6) | Only **pharmacologically relevant species**; immunogenicity; often one species; standard genotoxicity and carcinogenicity usually not applicable |
| Anticancer drugs (ICH S9) | Reduced package for patients with advanced cancer |

### d. Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)

Pivotal safety studies must follow **GLP**: the quality system for planning, performing, monitoring, recording, archiving and reporting non-clinical safety studies. USA: **21 CFR Part 58**; internationally: **OECD Principles of GLP**, with mutual acceptance of data among adhering countries. In India, the **National GLP Compliance Monitoring Authority (NGCMA)** certifies test facilities. Key GLP elements: study director (single point of control), quality assurance unit, approved protocol, SOPs, characterised test item, qualified facilities and equipment, raw data, final report and archives.

### e. Animal welfare

Studies are approved by an institutional animal ethics committee and follow the **3Rs**: replacement, reduction and refinement. In India animal experiments are controlled under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 through the national committee for control and supervision of experiments on animals (check the current name and rules on its website).

## 4.3 Timing of non-clinical studies (ICH M3(R2))

ICH M3(R2) links each clinical stage to the non-clinical data needed:

| Before … | Typical non-clinical data needed |
| --- | --- |
| First-in-human (Phase I) | Safety pharmacology core battery, repeat-dose toxicity in two species of at least the planned clinical duration, in vitro genotoxicity, ADME basics, local tolerance |
| Phase II / longer trials | Longer repeat-dose studies, complete genotoxicity battery, embryo-foetal studies before women of child-bearing potential are included (with regional differences) |
| Phase III and marketing | Chronic toxicity, full reproductive package, carcinogenicity (when needed) |

Exploratory clinical trials (microdosing, "Phase 0") can start with a reduced package, as described in ICH M3(R2).

## 4.4 Choosing the first human dose (principles only)

Two approaches are used:

1. **NOAEL-based approach (FDA guidance on estimating the maximum safe starting dose):** find the no-observed-adverse-effect level in each species → convert to a **human equivalent dose (HED)** using body-surface-area scaling → pick the most appropriate species → divide by a **safety factor** (default 10, increased when there is reason for concern) → maximum recommended starting dose.
2. **MABEL (minimal anticipated biological effect level):** used for high-risk products such as immune agonists, where pharmacology rather than toxicity drives risk; based on receptor binding and in vitro activity.

Sentinel dosing (one subject first, with observation before the rest of the cohort) is used for higher-risk first-in-human trials.

## 4.5 Global submission of the IND (and its equivalents)

### a. USA — Investigational New Drug application (21 CFR 312)

Contents under **21 CFR 312.23(a)**:

1. Cover sheet (**Form FDA 1571**).
2. Table of contents.
3. Introductory statement and general investigational plan.
4. (Reserved.)
5. Investigator's Brochure.
6. Protocols.
7. Chemistry, manufacturing and control information.
8. Pharmacology and toxicology information.
9. Previous human experience with the investigational drug.
10. Additional information (for example drug dependence and abuse potential, radioactive drugs, paediatric studies).
11. Other relevant information requested by FDA.

Each investigator signs **Form FDA 1572**. The IND goes into effect **30 days after FDA receives it** unless FDA imposes a **clinical hold**. Types: investigator IND, emergency use IND, treatment IND, commercial IND. Later filings: protocol amendments, information amendments, IND safety reports, annual reports.

### b. Other regions

| Region | Clinical trial application | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| European Union | **Clinical trial application** under **Regulation (EU) No 536/2014**, submitted once through **CTIS** for all chosen member states | Regulation applied from 31 January 2022; CTIS mandatory for new applications from 31 January 2023; transition of older trials ended 31 January 2025. Part I (scientific, coordinated by a reporting member state) and Part II (national and ethical aspects) assessment |
| UK | Combined review by MHRA and research ethics committee | Clinical trials regulations updated recently; check MHRA |
| Japan | Clinical trial notification to PMDA | Consultations with PMDA before filing |
| Canada | Clinical Trial Application (CTA) to Health Canada | Default review period set in the regulations |
| Australia | CTN (notification) or CTA (approval) scheme with the TGA | Most trials use CTN with ethics committee approval |
| India | Application in **Form CT-04** to the Central Licensing Authority; permission in **Form CT-06** | Decision within 90 working days; 30 working days for drugs discovered and developed in India; ethics committee approval and CTRI registration also needed |

### c. Strategy for global development

- Run **multi-regional clinical trials (ICH E17)** so one programme supports approval in many regions; consider ethnic factors (ICH E5).
- Seek scientific advice early (FDA meetings, EMA scientific advice, PMDA consultations, CDSCO pre-submission meetings).
- Keep one core data package; adapt Module 1 and local requirements.
- Plan paediatric development early (US Pediatric Study Plan; EU Paediatric Investigation Plan).

## 4.6 Global submission of the NDA and ANDA

### a. Marketing applications compared

| Region | New drug | Generic | Granted document |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| USA | NDA (505(b)(1)/(b)(2)); BLA | ANDA (505(j)); biosimilar 351(k) | Approval letter / licence |
| EU | Marketing authorisation application (MAA): centralised, decentralised, mutual recognition, national | Generic MAA (Article 10(1) of Directive 2001/83/EC); hybrid; biosimilar | Marketing authorisation |
| UK | MAA to MHRA (national or reliance route) | Generic MAA | Marketing authorisation |
| Japan | New drug application to MHLW/PMDA | Generic application | MHLW approval |
| Canada | New Drug Submission (NDS) | Abbreviated NDS | Notice of Compliance + DIN |
| Australia | Registration of new chemical entity | Generic registration | ARTG entry (AUST R) |
| India | CT-18 (import) / CT-21 (manufacture) to CLA | Application to CLA while still a "new drug"; afterwards State licence | Permission from CLA; licence |

### b. Typical sequence for a global NDA

```text
Core CTD (Modules 2–5) prepared once
 → USA: NDA via electronic gateway (eCTD) + PDUFA fee
 → EU: MAA via EMA (centralised) with EU Module 1, RMP, PIP compliance
 → Japan, Canada, Australia, Switzerland, others: regional Module 1
 → ROW: after a first approval, using COPP and reliance routes
 → Answer questions (FDA information requests, CHMP list of questions
   at day 120 and outstanding issues at day 180 in the EU)
 → Inspections → approvals → launch sequence
```

### c. Global ANDA / generic submissions

- Reference product differs by region (US RLD, EU reference medicinal product, national reference elsewhere); a BE study against one region's reference may not be accepted elsewhere unless allowed.
- Stability must cover the climatic zones of target markets.
- Patents and data/market protection differ: in the EU, generics follow the "8 + 2 (+1)" data and market protection rule; check current EU legislation, which was under revision.
- Labelling must follow each region's reference label.

## 4.7 Investigational Medicinal Product Dossier (IMPD)

**Definition:** the IMPD is the EU document that gives the **quality, manufacture and control** information on the investigational medicinal product (IMP), together with non-clinical and clinical data summaries where these are not in the Investigator's Brochure. It is submitted with a clinical trial application in the EU (the US IND gives similar information in its CMC and pharm/tox sections).

### a. Parts of an IMPD

| Part | Content |
| --- | --- |
| IMPD-Q (quality) | Drug substance: general information, manufacture, characterisation, control, reference standards, container closure, stability. Drug product: description and composition, pharmaceutical development, manufacture, control of excipients, control of product, container closure, stability. Placebo and comparator information |
| IMPD-S and E (safety and efficacy) | Summaries of non-clinical pharmacology, PK and toxicology, and of previous clinical data, with an overall benefit-risk assessment — may be replaced by cross-reference to the IB |

The quality part follows the CTD Module 3 structure, but the depth is **phase-appropriate**: early-phase IMPDs give provisional specifications and limited stability; later phases add more validation and data.

### b. Simplified IMPD

A shorter IMPD is allowed when the IMP is already authorised (in the EU or an ICH country) and used within or near its authorised conditions, or when data were submitted earlier by the same sponsor. Typically only the parts that have changed (for example re-packaging, blinding of a comparator) need full data.

### c. Related requirements

- IMPs are made under GMP for investigational products and released by a Qualified Person.
- Labelling of IMPs follows the clinical trials rules (trial reference, "for clinical trial use only", storage, sponsor).
- The IMPD is updated as the product and process change; substantial changes are submitted as modifications.

## 4.8 Investigator's Brochure (IB)

**Definition (ICH E6):** a compilation of the clinical and non-clinical data on the investigational product(s) that are relevant to its study in human subjects. Its purpose is to give investigators the information they need to understand the rationale for the protocol and to manage subjects safely: dose, frequency, administration and safety monitoring.

### a. Who writes and maintains it

The **sponsor** prepares the IB, keeps it up to date (reviewed at least once a year, and revised whenever important new information appears), and gives it to investigators and ethics committees. For a marketed product used in its approved way, the approved product information may replace the IB.

### b. Contents (ICH E6 outline)

1. Title page and confidentiality statement.
2. Table of contents.
3. **Summary** (physical, chemical, pharmaceutical, pharmacological, toxicological, PK, metabolic and clinical information).
4. **Introduction**: name, active ingredients, class, rationale, anticipated indications.
5. **Physical, chemical and pharmaceutical properties and formulation**, including storage and handling.
6. **Non-clinical studies**: pharmacology, PK and metabolism in animals, toxicology — with tables of findings and their relevance to humans.
7. **Effects in humans**: PK and metabolism, safety and efficacy, marketing experience.
8. **Summary of data and guidance for the investigator**: overall interpretation, possible risks and adverse reactions, precautions, special monitoring, and the **reference safety information (RSI)** used to decide whether a serious reaction is "expected".

The US rules list the same core: description of the drug substance and formulation; pharmacological and toxicological effects in animals and, if known, humans; pharmacokinetics and biological disposition; safety and effectiveness information from prior human studies; and anticipated risks and side effects with precautions or special monitoring (21 CFR 312.23(a)(5)).

### c. IB vs IMPD vs protocol

| Point | Investigator's Brochure | IMPD | Protocol |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audience | Investigators, ethics committees | Regulator (EU) | Everyone running the trial |
| Focus | Clinical and non-clinical data, risks, guidance | Quality of the IMP (+ summaries) | How this trial is run |
| Scope | The product (across trials) | The product as made for trials | One trial |
| Updated | At least yearly | When product/process changes | By amendment |

## 4.9 India: non-clinical and investigational requirements in brief

- The **NDCT Rules, 2019** set out the non-clinical data required for clinical trials and new drug applications in their schedules (pharmacology, toxicology, toxicokinetics, genotoxicity, reproductive and carcinogenicity data as appropriate).
- A clinical trial application includes the IB, protocol, informed consent documents, chemistry and manufacturing data, non-clinical data and, for global trials, data from other countries.
- Test licences permit manufacture or import of small quantities of a new drug for examination, testing or clinical trials.
- Applications go through the SUGAM portal; the Subject Expert Committee advises CDSCO.

## Remember

- Non-clinical aims: mechanism, toxicity profile, ADME, safe starting dose, clinical monitoring.
- Safety pharmacology core battery (S7A): CNS, cardiovascular, respiratory; QT: S7B + E14.
- Toxicology: single and repeat dose (two species), genotoxicity battery (S2), carcinogenicity (S1), reproductive (S5), biotech (S6, relevant species), anticancer (S9). Timing: ICH M3(R2).
- GLP: 21 CFR 58; OECD; India NGCMA; study director + QAU.
- First human dose: NOAEL → HED → safety factor; MABEL for high-risk biologics.
- IND contents 312.23(a)(1)–(11); Forms 1571 and 1572; 30-day rule; clinical hold.
- EU CTR 536/2014: applied 31 Jan 2022; CTIS mandatory for new trials from 31 Jan 2023; transition ended 31 Jan 2025; Part I / Part II.
- India: CT-04 → CT-06; 90/30 working days; CTRI.
- Global NDA: core CTD + regional Module 1; NDA, MAA, NDS, J-NDA; generics: ANDA, generic MAA, ANDS.
- IMPD: EU; quality (S + P) + summaries; phase-appropriate; simplified IMPD for authorised products.
- IB: sponsor's compilation for investigators; reviewed at least yearly; contains reference safety information.

# Unit 5: Clinical trials, ethics committees, informed consent, HIPAA and pharmacovigilance

This unit is PCI Unit 4. It covers how a **clinical trial protocol** is developed, how an **institutional review board (IRB) / independent ethics committee (IEC)** is formed and works, the **informed consent** process, the US **HIPAA** privacy requirements that affect clinical research, and **pharmacovigilance and safety monitoring** during trials.

Indian rules quoted here (ethics committee composition, safety reporting times, audio-video consent) come from the New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019 and match the B.Pharm notes (BP702T, BP804ET). US rules come from 21 CFR Parts 50, 56 and 312 and 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. Always check the current text before applying them.

## 5.1 Clinical trials: definitions, phases and the governing framework

A **clinical trial** is a systematic study of a new drug (or other intervention) in human subjects to generate data on its clinical, pharmacological (including pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic) or adverse effects, with the aim of establishing its safety and efficacy.

| Phase | Purpose | Typical subjects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 0 / exploratory | Microdose PK, target engagement | Very few, healthy volunteers or patients |
| Phase I | Safety, tolerability, PK, PD; dose escalation | Healthy volunteers (patients for cytotoxic drugs) |
| Phase II | Proof of concept, dose finding, short-term safety | Patients, limited number |
| Phase III | Confirm efficacy and safety in a larger, more varied population; basis for approval | Large patient numbers, often multicentre and multinational |
| Phase IV | After approval: long-term safety, new populations, comparative effectiveness | Patients in practice |

**Framework:** Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association); **ICH E6 Good Clinical Practice** (R3 adopted in 2025; Annex 2 added later); ICH E8(R1) general considerations (quality by design in trials); India — NDCT Rules 2019 and the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research; USA — 21 CFR 50, 56, 312, 812 and 45 CFR 46 (Common Rule) for federally funded research; EU — Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014.

### Principles of GCP (summarised)

1. Rights, safety and well-being of participants come first and prevail over the interests of science and society.
2. Informed consent is freely given and documented.
3. Independent ethics committee review.
4. Scientifically sound, clearly described trial design.
5. Qualified investigators and staff.
6. Quality built into design (identify factors critical to quality; proportionate, risk-based approach).
7. Reliable, accurate, traceable data; confidentiality protected.
8. Investigational products made under GMP and used per protocol.
9. Roles and responsibilities clear; sponsor keeps oversight even when tasks are delegated.

## 5.2 Developing clinical trial protocols

The **protocol** describes the objectives, design, methodology, statistical considerations and organisation of a trial. It must be approved by the regulator and the ethics committee before the trial starts, and changes are made only by approved **amendments**.

### a. Steps in protocol development

```text
Clinical question (from non-clinical data, earlier phases, unmet need)
 → Target product profile and regulatory advice (FDA/EMA/CDSCO meetings)
 → Literature review; feasibility (patients available, sites, standard of care)
 → Identify critical-to-quality factors and risks (ICH E8(R1), E6(R3))
 → Choose design, population, endpoints, comparator, sample size
 → Draft protocol + synopsis (clinicians, statisticians, PK, safety,
   regulatory, data management, QA, patient input where possible)
 → Internal review → CRF design → statistical analysis plan
 → Submission to regulator + ethics committee → approved version
 → Registration in a public registry (CTRI in India; ClinicalTrials.gov;
   EU CTIS) → amendments during the trial as needed
```

### b. Contents of a protocol

| Section | Includes |
| --- | --- |
| General information | Title, protocol number, version and date, sponsor, investigators, laboratories |
| Background and rationale | Product description, non-clinical and clinical findings, known and potential risks and benefits, justification of dose and route, population, references |
| Objectives and endpoints | Primary and secondary objectives; primary, secondary and exploratory endpoints; the estimand (what exactly is being estimated, ICH E9(R1)) |
| Design | Type (parallel, crossover, factorial, adaptive), control (placebo, active, historical), **randomisation**, **blinding**, treatment duration, stopping rules, accountability of IP, code-break procedure |
| Subjects | Inclusion, exclusion and withdrawal criteria; recruitment and follow-up |
| Treatment | IP and comparator, dosing schedule, permitted and prohibited concomitant medicines, compliance |
| Assessments | Efficacy measures, safety measures, schedule of assessments (visit table) |
| Safety | Definitions of AE/SAE, recording, causality, reporting timelines, follow-up |
| Statistics | Sample size and power, analysis sets (ITT, per-protocol, safety), methods, multiplicity, interim analyses, missing data |
| Data and quality | Source documents, data management, monitoring plan, audits |
| Ethics | Ethics committee approval, informed consent process, compensation and insurance |
| Administrative | Record retention, finance, publication policy, protocol amendments |

### c. Common design choices

- **Randomisation:** simple, block, stratified — removes selection bias.
- **Blinding:** open, single-blind, double-blind, double-dummy — removes assessment bias.
- **Control:** placebo (ethically acceptable only where no proven therapy is withheld to the patient's harm), active comparator, add-on design.
- **Superiority, non-inferiority, equivalence** hypotheses — each with its own margin and analysis.
- **Adaptive designs:** pre-planned changes (dose arms, sample size) based on interim data without undermining validity.

## 5.3 Institutional Review Board / Independent Ethics Committee: formation and working

An ethics committee is an **independent body** of medical, scientific and non-scientific members whose job is to protect the rights, safety and well-being of trial participants. In the USA it is the **IRB**; elsewhere the **IEC** or simply **ethics committee (EC)**.

### a. Formation (constitution)

| Requirement | India (NDCT Rules 2019, rule 7) | USA (21 CFR 56.107) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimum members | **7** | **5** |
| Composition | Medical, non-medical, scientific and non-scientific members, including at least one lay person, one woman, one legal expert, and one independent member from a related field (such as a social scientist, voluntary organisation representative, ethicist or theologian) | Varied backgrounds; at least one scientist, one non-scientist, one member not affiliated with the institution; not all of one sex or one profession |
| Independence | At least 50% of members not affiliated with the institute; chairperson not affiliated; member secretary affiliated | Members with a conflict of interest do not take part in that review |
| Registration | Registered with the Central Licensing Authority (application Form CT-01, registration Form CT-02) | IRBs register with HHS/FDA |
| Training | As specified by the CLA | Institution's responsibility |

### b. Working procedures

```text
Written SOPs (membership, quorum, meetings, review types, records)
 → Receive submission: protocol, IB, ICF and information sheet in local
   languages, CRFs, recruitment materials, investigator CVs and site
   details, insurance/compensation, regulatory status
 → Initial review in a quorate meeting (members with conflicts withdraw)
 → Decision: approve / approve with modifications / disapprove /
   suspend or terminate an earlier approval — communicated in writing
 → Continuing review (at least yearly in most systems): progress
   reports, amendments, deviations, new safety information
 → Safety review: SAEs, deaths, SUSARs; in India, opinion on
   compensation for trial-related injury or death
 → Site monitoring visits where needed
 → Final report review; archive records for the period set by the rules
```

**Expedited review** may be used for minor amendments or minimal-risk research, as the committee's SOPs allow. Committees must keep minutes, membership lists, SOPs, correspondence and decisions.

### c. Points the committee considers

Scientific validity (poor science is unethical), risk–benefit balance, fair selection of subjects and protection of vulnerable groups, adequacy and language of the consent documents, confidentiality, payment that is not coercive, compensation for injury, qualifications of the investigator and adequacy of the site.

## 5.4 Informed consent process and procedures

**Informed consent** is the process by which a subject voluntarily confirms willingness to take part in a trial after being informed of all aspects relevant to that decision. It is documented on a written, signed and dated form, but it is a **continuing process**, not a single signature.

### a. Elements of information (ICH E6; 21 CFR 50.25; Third Schedule of the NDCT Rules)

1. The trial involves research; purpose, duration and procedures; which procedures are experimental.
2. Trial treatments and the probability of random assignment.
3. Foreseeable risks and discomforts (including to an embryo or foetus where relevant).
4. Expected benefits, or that there may be none.
5. Alternative treatments.
6. Confidentiality of records and who may access them (monitors, auditors, ethics committee, regulators).
7. Compensation and treatment for trial-related injury.
8. Contacts for questions about the trial, subjects' rights and injury.
9. Participation is **voluntary**; refusal or withdrawal at any time without penalty or loss of benefits.
10. Circumstances in which the investigator may end participation; expected number of subjects; payments and expenses.

### b. Procedure

```text
Ethics-committee-approved ICF + information sheet in a language the
subject understands
 → Explained by the investigator or a trained delegate, in plain words
 → Time to read, think, ask questions and consult family
 → No coercion or undue influence
 → Signed and dated by subject (or legally acceptable representative)
   and by the person conducting the discussion; impartial witness if
   the subject cannot read
 → Copy given to the subject
 → Re-consent when significant new information arises or the
   protocol changes in a way that affects the subject
```

### c. Special situations

- **Children:** permission of parent or legally acceptable representative plus the child's **assent** when able to understand.
- **Incapable or unconscious adults:** consent of a legally acceptable representative; emergency research only as rules and the committee allow.
- **Illiterate subjects:** impartial witness present throughout.
- **India:** **audio-video recording** of the consent process is required for vulnerable subjects in trials of a new chemical entity or new molecular entity; for anti-HIV and anti-leprosy drug trials only an audio recording is kept (NDCT Rules 2019).
- **Re-use of samples and data:** consent must cover storage and future use, or fresh consent/committee approval is needed.

## 5.5 HIPAA and its requirements for the clinical study process

The **Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), 1996** is a US law. Its **Privacy Rule** (45 CFR Part 160 and Part 164, Subparts A and E) protects individually identifiable health information. Indian students study it because global trials that include US sites must comply with it; India's own counterpart is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, alongside the confidentiality duties in the NDCT Rules and ICMR guidelines.

### a. Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Covered entity | Health plans, health-care clearinghouses and health-care providers that transmit health information electronically (hospitals and clinics running trials usually are) |
| Protected health information (PHI) | Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity |
| Authorization | The individual's written permission for a specific use or disclosure of PHI for research |
| Privacy board | A board (alternative to the IRB) that can approve waivers of authorization |

A sponsor is not usually a covered entity itself, but it receives PHI from covered-entity sites, so HIPAA shapes what sites can send.

### b. Ways a researcher may use or disclose PHI

1. **With the subject's authorization** — usually a HIPAA authorization signed with (or within) the informed consent form, stating what PHI is used, by whom, for what purpose, an expiry, and the right to revoke.
2. **Waiver or alteration of authorization** approved by an **IRB or privacy board**: the research must pose no more than minimal risk to privacy (with a plan to protect identifiers, destroy them when possible, and not re-use them), and must be impracticable without the waiver and without the PHI.
3. **Reviews preparatory to research** (for example checking whether enough eligible patients exist): the researcher gives written assurance that PHI is used only for this, will not leave the covered entity, and is necessary.
4. **Research on decedents' information**, with similar assurances and, on request, proof of death.
5. **De-identified data** — not PHI at all. Two methods: **Safe Harbor** (remove **18 identifiers** — for example names, small geographic units, all date elements except year, phone and fax numbers, e-mail, social security, medical record and account numbers, device identifiers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers, full-face photographs and any other unique code — with no actual knowledge that the rest could identify the person) or **Expert Determination** (a qualified statistician documents that the risk of re-identification is very small).
6. **Limited data set** (direct identifiers removed but, for example, town, state, zip code and dates kept) with a **data use agreement** that limits use and forbids re-identification.

### c. Impact on the clinical study process

- Consent documents include HIPAA authorization language; IRBs check it.
- Monitors' access to source records is covered by the authorization.
- Subjects are coded (subject ID), and CRFs carry no direct identifiers.
- Security safeguards for electronic data (HIPAA Security Rule); breach notification duties.
- **Accounting of disclosures** for some research disclosures made without authorization.
- Subjects keep a right of access to their records (which can be suspended during a blinded trial if they agreed to this).

## 5.6 Pharmacovigilance: safety monitoring in clinical trials

**Pharmacovigilance (WHO):** the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. In trials, it protects subjects now and builds the safety profile used at approval.

### a. Definitions (ICH E2A)

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Adverse event (AE) | Any untoward medical occurrence in a subject given a pharmaceutical product, not necessarily caused by it |
| Adverse drug reaction (ADR) | Noxious and unintended response where a causal relationship is at least a reasonable possibility |
| Serious | Results in death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalisation, causes persistent or significant disability/incapacity, or a congenital anomaly/birth defect; or other medically important event |
| Unexpected | Nature or severity not consistent with the reference safety information (IB or label) |
| SUSAR | Suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction |

Severity (mild, moderate, severe) describes intensity; **seriousness** is the regulatory criterion for reporting.

### b. Safety monitoring flow

```text
Event detected (subject report, visit, lab result)
 → Recorded in source and CRF: onset, severity, seriousness, action, outcome
 → Investigator assesses seriousness and causality (WHO-UMC or similar)
 → Serious → reported quickly to sponsor (and in India also to CLA and EC)
 → Sponsor: medical review, expectedness against RSI, coding (MedDRA),
   case report in E2B format → expedited reports to regulators,
   investigators and ethics committees
 → Aggregate review: safety review team, DSMB, signal detection
 → Actions: IB update, protocol amendment, consent update,
   dose change, enrolment pause, trial stop
 → Periodic report: DSUR (ICH E2F), yearly
```

### c. Reporting timelines

| System | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| ICH E2A | Fatal or life-threatening SUSARs: as soon as possible, within **7 calendar days** of first knowledge (follow-up within 8 more days); other SUSARs within **15 calendar days** |
| USA (21 CFR 312.32) | IND safety reports within 15 calendar days; unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions within 7 calendar days |
| India (NDCT Rules 2019) | Investigator reports every **SAE** to the CLA, sponsor and ethics committee **within 24 hours**; the analysed report goes to the CLA, ethics committee chairperson and head of institution **within 14 days**; reasons needed for delays. Deaths are examined by an independent expert committee, which also advises on compensation |

### d. Roles in safety monitoring

| Role | Safety duties |
| --- | --- |
| Investigator | Detect, record, treat and report AEs/SAEs; follow up to resolution; inform EC |
| Sponsor | Continuous safety evaluation; expedited and periodic reporting; update IB; set up DSMB when needed; provide compensation (India) |
| Monitor (CRA) | Checks AEs in source are captured in CRFs and reported on time |
| Ethics committee | Reviews SAEs and new safety data; can suspend approval |
| DSMB / DMC | Independent experts reviewing unblinded accumulating data; recommends continue, modify or stop |
| Regulator | Reviews reports, inspects, can impose clinical hold or suspend |

### e. Causality assessment

Common methods: **WHO-UMC system** (certain, probable/likely, possible, unlikely, conditional/unclassified, unassessable/unclassifiable) and the **Naranjo algorithm** (questionnaire scoring: definite, probable, possible, doubtful). Factors: time relationship, dechallenge and rechallenge, alternative causes, known pharmacology, plausibility.

### f. From trials to the market

Safety data collected in development feed the **risk management plan (RMP)** in the EU and **REMS** in the USA, and in India the post-approval PSURs (six-monthly for two years, then yearly for two years). Spontaneous reporting continues through **PvPI** (Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad), MedWatch/FAERS (USA) and the Yellow Card scheme (UK). The **DSUR** (ICH E2F) is the yearly development safety report; after approval the **PBRER** (ICH E2C(R2)) takes over in many regions.

## 5.7 Compensation, registration and quality in Indian trials (quick facts)

- Sponsor must provide **medical management** and **compensation** for trial-related injury or death; the amount follows the formula in the NDCT Rules.
- Trials must be registered in the **Clinical Trials Registry – India (CTRI)** before the first subject is enrolled.
- CDSCO inspects sites, sponsors and CROs; findings can lead to rejection of data, suspension or debarment.
- Records are kept for the period specified in the rules.

## Remember

- Phases 0–IV; GCP (ICH E6, R3 2025): participant first, consent, EC review, sound design, quality by design, reliable data.
- Protocol: background, objectives/endpoints (estimand), design (randomisation, blinding, control), subjects, treatment, assessments, safety, statistics, data/quality, ethics, administration.
- EC India: ≥7 members (lay person, woman, legal expert, independent member), ≥50% non-affiliated, non-affiliated chair; CT-01 → CT-02. US IRB: ≥5 (scientist, non-scientist, non-affiliated).
- EC decisions: approve, approve with modifications, disapprove, suspend/terminate; continuing review; SAE review.
- Informed consent: process; 10 core elements; LAR, assent, impartial witness; India audio-video for vulnerable subjects in NCE/NME trials.
- HIPAA (45 CFR 160, 164): PHI, covered entity; authorization; IRB/privacy board waiver; preparatory to research; decedents; de-identification (Safe Harbor 18 identifiers or expert determination); limited data set + data use agreement.
- PV: AE, ADR, serious, unexpected, SUSAR. ICH 7/15 days; US 312.32; India SAE 24 hours + 14 days. DSUR yearly; DSMB; WHO-UMC and Naranjo causality.
- India: compensation formula, CTRI before first enrolment, PSURs 6-monthly × 2 y then yearly × 2 y, PvPI at IPC Ghaziabad.
